Permutations, Pattern Covers, Posets and Positivity: Part I: Patterns and Posets

Natasha Blitvić ††thanks: n.blitvic@qmul.ac.uk. Partially supported by Leverhulme Trust Research Project Grant RPG-2020-103 and the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC) grant EP/V048902. Affiliation: School of Mathematical Sciences, Queen Mary University of London    Mohammed Slim Kammoun ††thanks: medslimkammoun@gmail.com. Partially supported by Leverhulme Trust Research Project Grant RPG-2020-103, CNRS-INSMI PEPS JCJC projects LAMPE and CAPRICES, LabEx CIMI (ANR-11-LABX-0040), and ANR project LOUCCOUM (ANR-24-CE40-7809). Affiliation: Université de Poitiers, CNRS, LMA    Einar Steingrímsson ††thanks: einar@alum.mit.edu Affiliation: Department of Mathematics and Statistics, University of Strathclyde
Abstract

We study permutations covered by occurrences of a consecutive permutation pattern, with successive occurrences overlapping in a fixed number of positions. Several special cases of this construction have been studied in the theory of consecutive patterns and via the cluster method. Here we study the sequences obtained by repeating a fixed overlap. We elicit many structural properties of such pattern covers, mainly in terms of posets whose linear extensions are in bijection with the permutations in question. The enumeration of these permutations for different patterns gives rise to a great variety of sequences, many classical, but most of them not found in the OEIS. We conjecture that, with minor modifications, all of these sequences are moments of probability measures on the real line.

We develop a general enumerative and order-theoretic framework for these objects. For overlap one, we give a generating function whose coefficients enumerate permutations covered by an arbitrary fixed pattern with any prescribed number of occurrences. For every overlap at most half the length of the pattern, we derive a recursive formula which, for fixed pattern and overlap, yields a polynomial-time enumeration algorithm. We then associate to each pattern, overlap, and number of occurrences a naturally defined poset whose linear extensions are in bijection with the corresponding pattern-covered permutations.

The regularity of this poset construction makes possible a structural analysis that in many cases leads to enumerative formulas for large classes of patterns. We prove uniform restrictions on the local structure of the Hasse diagrams, describe their branches (pendant chains) in terms of the corresponding patterns, and characterize when the poset is a tree (seen as an undirected graph) or chain.

We also construct patterns whose Hasse diagrams have a simple grid-like structure. Some of these results yield explicit families of formulas, explain unexpected equinumerations, and exhibit classes of new enumerative phenomena in consecutive permutation patterns.

In a forthcoming companion paper [2], we investigate the sequences arising here from a probabilistic perspective, viewing them both as point processes and as moment sequences. We also obtain integral and matrix representations for important overlap 11 and 22 classes of pattern-covering sequences.

1 Introduction

Let 𝒮ℓ\mathcal{S}_{\ell} be the set of permutations of the set {1,2,…,ℓ}\{1,2,\ldots,\ell\}. Given permutations π∈𝒮K\pi\in\mathcal{S}_{K} and σ∈𝒮n\sigma\in\mathcal{S}_{n}, an occurrence of the pattern π\pi in σ\sigma is obtained by selecting entries of σ\sigma whose relative order is the same as that of π\pi. If the selected entries are required to occupy consecutive positions, then π\pi is called a consecutive pattern. The systematic study of permutation patterns has its origins in work of Knuth and of Simion and Schmidt [12, 15]. For some background on consecutive patterns, see [16].

Two occurrences of a consecutive pattern containing some of the same entries of a permutation impose order conditions on these entries, beyond what each occurrence must satisfy. Thus the enumeration is not determined merely by the length and structure of the pattern or by the number of occurrences: it depends on how two copies of that particular pattern can fit together, at the beginning of one and the end of the other. Cluster methods and related generating-function techniques have provided the principal general framework for studying these interactions [3, 8, 10, 11, 13]. The role of overlap also underlies refined notions of consecutive Wilf equivalence (two patterns having the same enumeration) and the study of patterns two of whose occurrences can overlap in at most one entry of a permutation [4, 5].

In this paper, we require successive occurrences of a consecutive pattern in a permutation σ\sigma to overlap in exactly mm entries for some given mm, and study the structure of such permutations and their enumeration. Concretely, fix a pattern π∈𝒮K\pi\in\mathcal{S}_{K}, an overlap m<Km<K, and j≥1j\geq 1, the prescribed number of occurrences. We count permutations σ∈𝒮n\sigma\in\mathcal{S}_{n} containing occurrences of π\pi beginning at

1,1+(K−m),1+2​(K−m),…,1+(j−1)​(K−m),1,1+(K-m),1+2(K-m),\ldots,1+(j-1)(K-m),

so that every two successive prescribed occurrences overlap in exactly mm positions, and every entry of σ\sigma belongs to some occurrence. These conditions of course constrain the size of the permutation σ\sigma to be n=K+(j−1)​(K−m)n=K+(j-1)(K-m). We call such corresponding permutations pattern packings and denote their count by Nπm​(j)N_{\pi}^{m}(j). (Note that we disregard potential occurrences outside the prescribed ones.)

The individual numbers Nπm​(j)N_{\pi}^{m}(j) are instances of the refined cluster numbers studied by Dwyer and Elizalde [5], where occurrences may be prescribed at an arbitrary set of starting positions. Here we instead systematically study the constant-overlap specialization in which the starting positions form an arithmetic progression and the number of prescribed occurrences varies.

Because the same overlap is repeated at every step, a packing with j+1j+1 occurrences is obtained from one with jj occurrences by adjoining another copy of the same local configuration. Although adding a new copy in this way typically allows for rearrangement of the previous entries, this highlights a recursive structure that can in many cases be exploited for understanding of the global structure and for enumeration of the permutations in question, even though it does not make the enumeration uniformly simple. Even for short patterns, the sequences

(Nπm​(j))j≥1\bigl(N_{\pi}^{m}(j)\bigr)_{j\geq 1}

display strikingly different behavior. Some are given by Catalan or Fuss–Catalan numbers, some by products of factorials or binomial coefficients, and most appear not to belong to previously studied families. Small changes in the pattern may alter the sequence substantially, while quite different patterns may unexpectedly produce the same sequence. The problem is therefore to understand how much of this variation can be explained by general mechanisms, rather than by a separate argument for each pattern.

The covering of permutations by occurrences of a consecutive pattern partly generalizes the notion of the descent set, which is the set of starting positions of descents in a permutation, that is, positions ii such that σ⁡(i)>σ⁡(i+1)\sigma(i)>\sigma(i+1), which is simply an occurrence of the consecutive pattern 21. In a seminal paper [9] Gessel and Viennot gave a formula, in terms of determinants, for the number of permutations in 𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{n} with any given descent set (a special case of the celebrated Lindström-Gessel-Viennot Lemma). A general formula for the number of permutations with any set of starting points for a given consecutive pattern seems out of reach, given how hard the general problem is for a single pattern occurring at regular intervals. The only case we present here that goes beyond regular intervals and overlaps involves patterns whose occurrences are allowed to overlap in either one or two places, see Proposition 6.1.

The first part of the paper develops such mechanisms on the enumerative side. We establish symmetries that preserve the packing numbers and identify further transformations specific to a fixed overlap. For overlap m=1m=1, where the enumeration depends only on the first and last entry of a pattern, we express Nπ1​(j)N_{\pi}^{1}(j) as a coefficient of a single multivariate formal power series.

For general overlap satisfying m≤K/2m\leq K/2, we derive a recurrence by analyzing the effect of adding a new occurrence and how that allows for rearrangement of the previous entries. For each such pair (π,m)(\pi,m) the recurrence gives an algorithm for computing Nπm​(j)N_{\pi}^{m}(j) as jj varies. This algorithm is very effective for m=1m=1, but less so for greater mm.

The second part of the paper develops an order-theoretic approach to the same problem. Each occurrence of π\pi imposes a chain of inequalities among the entries occupying its positions. Superimposing the chains from the prescribed occurrences produces a finite poset, which we call the pattern-packing poset and denote by 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j). Its linear extensions are naturally in bijection with the corresponding pattern packings, so that

Nπm​(j)=|ℒ⁡(𝒫πm​(j))|,N_{\pi}^{m}(j)=\left|\mathcal{L}\bigl({\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j)\bigr)\right|,

where ℒ⁡(𝒫πm​(j))\mathcal{L}({\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j)) is the set of linear extensions of 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j).

Special cases of these posets, encoding the inequalities imposed by prescribed overlapping occurrences, arise in cluster constructions and in the framework of [3, 5, 8]. Here we treat the constant-overlap posets as a sequence indexed by jj and exploit the repeated structure arising from the regularly spaced starting positions of occurrences.

To make that structure visible, we introduce a stack representation in which each prescribed occurrence contributes a translated copy of the same chain, and overlapping positions are identified. Although the defining chains are individually simple, their transitive closure can produce complicated structures. In particular, repeated local constraints may create undirected cycles, branching, interleaving, or grid-like regions in the Hasse diagram. This is another manifestation of the central difficulty: the local rule is specified by a single permutation, but its repeated application can generate a much less transparent global order.

We prove several restrictions valid for every pattern-packing poset. Each element is covered by at most two elements and covers at most two elements, and the poset decomposes into a core —which is a lattice bounded by elements that belong to every chain of maximal length — and (possibly) chain components attached to the core by single edges. We then characterize several distinguished families depending on the structure of their Hasse diagrams and the corresponding undirected graph, which in many cases leads to enumerative formulas. We give necessary and sufficient conditions for the Hasse diagram to be a tree, and, when m≤K/2m\leq K/2, express these conditions directly in terms of the prefix and suffix of the pattern. We similarly characterize the case where the poset is a chain, and construct a class of patterns whose packing posets form shifted grids, posets obtained from rectangular subsets of the integer lattice ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} by shifting hh steps to the right the unit rectangles at height hh. These classifications identify finite features of the pattern that control the structure of the entire family

𝒫πm​(1),𝒫πm​(2),𝒫πm​(3),….{\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(1),{\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(2),{\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(3),\ldots.

The poset viewpoint also clarifies many equinumerations observed among the enumerating sequences. Some arise from elementary symmetries of the patterns, some from isomorphisms of the associated posets, and some from two posets differing in ways that leave the number of linear extensions invariant for trivial reasons. However, we also find pairs of patterns with identical packing sequences despite having nonisomorphic posets with visibly different structures, including examples in which one Hasse diagram is a tree and the other contains cycles, and even such pairs of patterns of different lengths and overlaps. Such examples indicate that the constant-overlap setting has a substantial equivalence theory that is not yet fully understood.

Wilf equivalences have been much studied for pattern avoidance. In our setting it seems to be much richer, since such equinumerations are not restricted to patterns of the same length and the same overlap. We present several such cases that are easily proved, but those only seem to scratch the surface.

Some of the results presented here were presented in our extended abstract [1] for the conference fpsac in 2023.

In a forthcoming companion paper [2], we study the sequences arising here as point processes and moment sequences. Using probabilistic methods, we derive integral and matrix representations for important overlap-11 and overlap-22 families. We further conjecture, and for many families are able to prove, that the pattern-packing uniformly gives rise to moments of probability measures on the real line. This not only identifies natural new connections between permutation patterns and probability theory, but also opens up more general approaches in a field of combinatorics where structure remains pattern-dependent.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 formally defines the relevant objects and establishes the notation. In Section 3 we establish symmetries of the packing numbers and discuss their relation to consecutive Wilf equivalence. Section 4 contains the coefficient-extraction formula for overlap one and the recurrence for overlaps at most half the pattern length. Section 5 introduces the pattern-packing posets and develops their structural theory, including the core-and-branch decomposition, the tree and chain criteria, and the shifted-grid construction. In Section 6 we mention one case of permutations covered by irregularly spaced occurrences of a pattern, with overlaps either 1 or 2. Finally, Section 7 presents open problems concerning further Wilf equivalences, extremal packing numbers, and other structural properties of pattern-packing posets than those we treat explicitly.

2 First Definitions and Notation

As is habitual in combinatorics, we let [n]:={1,…,n}[n]:=\{1,\ldots,n\} and denote by 𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{n} the set of all bijections [n]→[n][n]\to[n]. The set 𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{n} forms a group (the symmetric group) under functional composition ∘\circ, with the identity permutation as the identity element.

The study of permutation patterns is predominantly combinatorial, with the group structure rarely playing a role. Results in this area are typically formulated in the language of words, where 𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{n} is the set of permutations of {1,2,…,n}\{1,2,\ldots,n\}, that is, the elements of the symmetric group:

Definition 2.1 (Permutations as words (the one-line notation)).

We interpret elements of 𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{n} as words of length nn in the alphabet [n][n] formed of distinct letters. We write σ=σ1​…​σn\sigma=\sigma_{1}\ldots\sigma_{n} and refer to this as the one-line notation. For σ\sigma a word of length nn and σ′\sigma^{\prime} a word of length n′n^{\prime}, we denote by σ​σ′\sigma\sigma^{\prime} their concatenation, that is, the word of length n+n′n+n^{\prime} whose first nn letters are a copy of σ\sigma and the remaining n′n^{\prime} letters are a copy of σ′\sigma^{\prime}.

When talking about patterns and permutations in one-line notation we will interchangeably talk about their letters and elements.

When necessary, we mix the two interpretations of permutations. For example, σi−1\sigma^{-1}_{i} denotes the iith letter, in the one-line notation, of the functional inverse of σ\sigma.

Definition 2.2.

Given words ww and w′w^{\prime} of length ℓ\ell on the alphabet [n][n], we say that ww and w′w^{\prime} are order isomorphic, denoted w∼w′w\sim w^{\prime}, if for every i,j∈[ℓ]i,j\in[\ell], wi<wjw_{i}<w_{j} if and only if wi′<wj′w_{i}^{\prime}<w_{j}^{\prime}.

For example, 4936 is order isomorphic to 2413.

We now consider ways in which two permutations can be compared to one another by inclusion.

Definition 2.3 (Permutation Patterns).

Fix KK and π∈𝒮K\pi\in\mathcal{S}_{K}. For any σ∈𝒮n\sigma\in\mathcal{S}_{n}, where n≥Kn\geq K, we say that a tuple of indices (i1,…,iK)(i_{1},\ldots,i_{K}), with 1≤i1<i2<⋯<iK≤n1\leq i_{1}<i_{2}<\cdots<i_{K}\leq n, forms an occurrence of the classical permutation pattern π\pi if the word formed by restricting σ\sigma to indices i1,…,iKi_{1},\ldots,i_{K} is isomorphic to π\pi, that is, σi1​…​σiK∼π\sigma_{i_{1}}\ldots\sigma_{i_{K}}\sim\pi.

In contrast, for (i1,…,iK)(i_{1},\ldots,i_{K}) to form an occurrence in σ\sigma of the consecutive permutation pattern π\pi, the indices must be consecutive, that is, iK=iK−1+1=⋯=i1+K−1i_{K}=i_{K-1}+1=\cdots=i_{1}+K-1, so that the occurrence is a contiguous subword of σ\sigma.

The indices i1,…,iKi_{1},\ldots,i_{K} are referred to as the positions or places of the occurrence, with i1i_{1} being the starting position. □\square

Remark 2.4.

There is a more general inclusion rule that interpolates between the classical and consecutive patterns. These are the vincular patterns [16] (previously called generalized patterns), which we don’t consider here.

When a permutation σ\sigma contains no occurrences of a pattern π\pi, we say that σ\sigma avoids π\pi (or is an avoider of π\pi). A central question in the study of permutation patterns is this: Given a pattern π\pi, how many permutations σ∈𝒮n\sigma\in\mathcal{S}_{n} avoid π\pi (for any given nn)? Here, instead, we count permutations with occurrences of a given consecutive pattern appearing at regular, overlapping intervals.

2.1 Main objects

Henceforth, ’pattern’ will refer to a consecutive permutation pattern. Furthermore, as the size of the pattern will recur in the indexation and enumeration of various quantities, we assign it a capital letter and make it an explicit definition:

Definition 2.5.

A KK-pattern is a consecutive permutation pattern π∈𝒮K\pi\in\mathcal{S}_{K}.

The following is the main definition of this paper.

Definition 2.6 (Pattern packing).

Fix K≥2K\geq 2, j≥1j\geq 1, π\pi a KK-pattern, and 1≤m<K1\leq m<K. We say that a permutation σ∈𝒮n\sigma\in\mathcal{S}_{n} mm-packs jj occurrences of π\pi or that σ\sigma (m,j)(m,j)-packs π\pi if n=K+(j−1)​(K−m)n=K+(j-1)(K-m) and σ\sigma contains occurrences of π\pi starting in positions {1,1+d,1+2​d,…,1+(j−1)​d}\{1,1+d,1+2d,\ldots,1+(j-1)d\}, where d=K−md=K-m. In other words,

σ1+(i−1)​d​…​σK+(i−1)​d∼π,\sigma_{1+(i-1)d}\ldots\sigma_{K+(i-1)d}\;\sim\;\pi, (2.1)

where ∼\sim is order isomorphism and ii runs from 1 to jj. We also say that π\pi covers σ\sigma with overlaps mm, or that σ\sigma is mm-covered by π\pi, when the number of occurrences need not be specified.

Remark 2.7.

Definition 2.6 does not preclude additional occurrences, outside of the regularly occurring ones. For example, the permutation 192837465 1-packs 2 occurrences of 15243 since it contains occurrences of 15243 starting in positions 1 and 5. But it also contains an occurrence of 15243 starting in position 3, which we do not prohibit. Whether it is possible to have additional occurrences of a pattern depends on the length of the pattern π\pi, the length of the overlaps and the autocorrelation of π\pi, that is, the maximum possible overlap of two distinct occurrences of π\pi in a permutation. In order for a KK-pattern π\pi to possibly occur in more places in a permutation than those prescribed by overlaps m≥1m\geq 1, π\pi must have autocorrelation at least (K+m)/2(K+m)/2. In the remainder of the paper, an ’occurrence’ will always refer to one of the regular occurrences, that is, those starting in positions {1,1+d,1+2​d,…,1+(j−1)​d}\{1,1+d,1+2d,\ldots,1+(j-1)d\}, where d=K−md=K-m.

Remark 2.8.

The Main Definition focuses on the case where the regular occurrences overlap (that is, 1≤m<K1\leq m<K). However, allowing regular gaps between occurrences (which we can interpret as letting m<0m<0), or having occurrences adjacent without overlap (m=0m=0), simply adds trivially computed multiplicative factors to any enumerative formula.

2.2 Symmetries and Wilf equivalences

In pattern avoidance, two patterns π\pi and π′\pi^{\prime} are said to be Wilf equivalent if, for all nn, the subset of 𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{n} that avoids π\pi has the same size as that avoiding π′\pi^{\prime}. Some such equivalences are proved simply by applying the same symmetry operation on both a pattern and the permutations avoiding it, such as reversing both, or taking complements, which involves replacing the letter ii in a permutation/pattern of length nn by n+1−in+1-i.

Both of the above mentioned operations also preserve enumeration in the case of the pattern packing studied here, but there are a few others that apply to all patterns given a fixed overlap. For example, if the overlap mm is at most K/2K/2 for a KK-pattern then pattern-packing enumeration is invariant under the action of switching the mm-suffix and mm-prefix (Lemma 3.10), as well as permuting the mm-prefix and mm-suffix of a KK-pattern in the same way (Lemma 3.8). In addition to these, and some further general symmetries listed in Section 3, there seem to be myriad cases of pattern/overlap combinations with the same enumeration without falling under any of these general symmetries. Such equinumerations occur both when we fix pattern length and overlap length and for pairs of patterns of different lengths and with different overlaps, whereas for avoidance of single patterns, Wilf equivalence is only possible for patterns of the same length.

In Section 7 we mention several conjectured Wilf equivalences that do not fall under any of the general symmetries we exhibit in Section 3.

2.3 Pattern-packing posets and enumerating their linear extensions

In Section 5, we show that the inequalities satisfied by the elements of a permutation mm-packing a pattern π\pi give rise to a poset, which we term a pattern-packing poset (not to be confused with the posets in [6] and earlier papers cited there). These posets have previously been described for certain classes of patterns by Dotsenko and Khoroshkin [3] and by Elizalde and Noy [8]. While the structure of such a poset depends on the underlying pattern, the pattern-packing posets enjoy some general properties. For example, an element in such a poset can cover (and be covered by) at most two elements. Furthermore, due to the regularity of the underlying construction (Definition 2.6), these posets themselves exhibit regularity. As a result, pattern-packing posets can be classified according to the structure of their Hasse diagrams. In particular, we characterize patterns that give rise to trees (Theorem 5.20), and construct patterns realizing multilevel grids (Theorem 5.33).

For a given pattern π\pi, the number of permutations mm-packing jj occurrences of π\pi equals the number of linear extensions of a poset defined in terms of π\pi, mm and jj. The regularity of the pattern-packing posets enables us in some cases to explicitly count their linear extensions, developing methods that we present in Section 5. The enumerative results take the form of:

  • ∙\bullet

    A polynomial-time algorithm, for any overlap m≤K/2m\leq K/2. (Theorem 4.7.)

  • ∙\bullet

    A generating function, whenever m=1m=1. (Theorem 4.1.)

  • ∙\bullet

    Explicit enumeration formulas for specific families.

  • ∙\bullet

    Various integral formulas and matrix product formulas for general classes of patterns (to appear in our forthcoming companion paper [2] to this one).

In Figures 2.1 and 2.2, we show examples of posets for a variety of patterns and overlaps, and in Table 1 we list the enumeration of all pattern-overlap combinations for patterns of length at most 5, up to the trivial equivalences given in Section 3. All of these where a formula is known are special cases of more general results, to appear in Section 5.

3 Symmetries

Prior to moving into the classification and enumeration of permutations packing a given pattern — or, equivalently, the enumeration of linear extensions of pattern posets — we take note of a number of elementary symmetries that will simplify the task.

Definition 3.1.

Consider a permutation π∈𝒮n\pi\in\mathcal{S}_{n}, written as a word in one-line notation π1​…​πn\pi_{1}\ldots\pi_{n}. The reverse of π\pi is the permutation πR=πn​…​π1\pi^{R}=\pi_{n}\ldots\pi_{1}. The complement of π\pi is the permutation πC=(n+1−π1)​…​(n+1−πn)\pi^{C}=(n+1-\pi_{1})\ldots(n+1-\pi_{n}). The reverse complement of π\pi is obtained by composing the two operations, namely πR​C=(n+1−πn)​…​(n+1−π1)\pi^{RC}=(n+1-\pi_{n})\ldots(n+1-\pi_{1}).

Let 𝒮πm​(j)\mathcal{S}_{\pi}^{m}(j) denote the set of permutations mm-packing jj occurrences of a KK-pattern π\pi. The proof of the following lemma consists of applying the same symmetry operation to each permutation σ\sigma mm-packing a pattern π\pi as is applied to π\pi itself, since each of them transforms an occurrence of π\pi in σ\sigma in the same way as it transforms π\pi.

Lemma 3.2.

Fix a KK-pattern π\pi. Then, for any overlap mm and number of occurrences jj,

|𝒮πm​(j)|=|𝒮πRm​(j)|=|𝒮πCm​(j)|=|𝒮πR​Cm​(j)|.|\mathcal{S}_{\pi}^{m}(j)|=|\mathcal{S}_{\pi^{R}}^{m}(j)|=|\mathcal{S}_{\pi^{C}}^{m}(j)|=|\mathcal{S}_{\pi^{RC}}^{m}(j)|.

For example, for any given overlap mm, the number of permutations mm-packing 14253 is the same as that mm-packing any of the following patterns:

Nevertheless, a closer inspection of Table 1 reveals many more equinumerations than these trivial ones. Prior to discussing these, we require some additional notation.

Definition 3.3.

Let π\pi be a KK-pattern and m<Km<K. Its mm-prefix and mm-suffix are 𝐩=𝐩1​…​𝐩m=π1​…​πm\mathbf{p}=\mathbf{p}_{1}\ldots\mathbf{p}_{m}=\pi_{1}\ldots\pi_{m} and 𝐬=𝐬1​…​𝐬m=πK−m+1​…​πK\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}_{1}\ldots\mathbf{s}_{m}=\pi_{K-m+1}\ldots\pi_{K}, respectively. For m≤K/2m\leq K/2, its interfix is 𝐰=πm+1​…​πK−m\mathbf{w}=\pi_{m+1}\ldots\pi_{K-m}.

The interfix is empty when K=2​mK=2m. For j≥2j\geq 2, a packing can exist only if 𝐩∼𝐬\mathbf{p}\sim\mathbf{s}, since the orders imposed on each shared block must agree. If this fails, |𝒮πm​(1)|=1|\mathcal{S}_{\pi}^{m}(1)|=1 and |𝒮πm​(j)|=0|\mathcal{S}_{\pi}^{m}(j)|=0 for j≥2j\geq 2. Henceforth, whenever pattern packing is considered, we assume 𝐩∼𝐬\mathbf{p}\sim\mathbf{s}.

Any permutation σ\sigma (m,j)(m,j)-packing a KK-pattern π\pi naturally decomposes into distinct subwords. Namely, if m>K/2m>K/2 the subwords corresponding to the overlap of the prefix and the suffix are necessarily order isomorphic to the intersection of the prefix and suffix. In contrast, when m≤K/2m\leq K/2, the packing does not place further constraints on the jj subwords that lie between the prefix/suffix components, apart from having to be isomorphic to the interfix of π\pi. We denote the resulting decomposition as follows.

Notation 3.4.

[Decomposition of permutations packing a pattern] Fix a KK-pattern π\pi and overlap m≤K/2m\leq K/2. For j∈ℕj\in\mathbb{N} and σ∈𝒮πm​(j)\sigma\in\mathcal{S}_{\pi}^{m}(j), we write

σ=ρ(1)​ω(1)​ρ(2)​ω(2)​…​ρ(j)​ω(j)​ρ(j+1),\sigma=\rho^{(1)}\omega^{(1)}\rho^{(2)}\omega^{(2)}\ldots\rho^{(j)}\omega^{(j)}\rho^{(j+1)}, (3.1)

where, for all i∈[j+1]i\in[j+1], ρ(i)∼𝐩\rho^{(i)}\sim\mathbf{p}, that is, each ρ(i)\rho^{(i)} must be isomorphic to the mm-prefix/suffix of π\pi. When m=K/2m=K/2 the ω(i)\omega^{(i)} are empty, in which case σ\sigma also packs j+1j+1 non-overlapping occurrences of the mm-prefix/suffix of π\pi.

Example 3.5.

For σ=1   11   5  2   10   7   3  9   6   4   8∈𝒮153242​(3)\sigma=1\,\,\,11\,\,\,5\,\,2\,\,\,10\,\,\,7\,\,\,3\,\,9\,\,\,6\,\,\,4\,\,\,8\in\mathcal{S}_{15324}^{2}(3), we have

σ=1    11⏟ρ(1)​5⏟ω(1)​2     10⏟ρ(2)​7⏟ω(2)​3      9⏟ρ(3)​6⏟ω(3)​4      8⏟ρ(4).\sigma=\underbrace{1\,\,\,\,11}_{\rho^{(1)}}\,\underbrace{5}_{\omega^{(1)}}\,\underbrace{2\,\,\,\,\,10}_{\rho^{(2)}}\,\underbrace{7}_{\omega^{(2)}}\,\underbrace{3\,\,\,\,\,\,9}_{\rho^{(3)}}\,\underbrace{6}_{\omega^{(3)}}\,\underbrace{4\,\,\,\,\,\,8}_{\rho^{(4)}}.

When we talk about permuting a word w1​w2​…​wnw_{1}w_{2}\ldots w_{n} consisting of distinct letters by a permutation τ=τ1​τ2​…​τn\tau=\tau_{1}\tau_{2}\ldots\tau_{n} that means arranging the letters of ww so that wτiw_{\tau_{i}} is in place ii in the permuted word. For example, permuting 46927 by 31542 results in 94726.

For fixed overlap mm, we can now state the following additional symmetry.

Lemma 3.6.

The number of permutations (m,j)(m,j)-packing a KK-pattern π\pi depends only on the mm-prefix and mm-suffix of π\pi.

Proof.

When m≥K/2m\geq K/2, the result is trivial because one can then reconstruct π\pi from its mm-prefix and mm-suffix, which between them contain all the letters of π\pi. Suppose now that m<K/2m<K/2. Let π=𝐩𝐰𝐬\pi=\mathbf{p}\mathbf{w}\mathbf{s}, interpreted as a word and written as the concatenation of the mm-prefix 𝐩\mathbf{p}, the interfix 𝐰\mathbf{w}, and the mm-suffix 𝐬\mathbf{s}. Any permutation σ∈𝒮πm​(j)\sigma\in\mathcal{S}_{\pi}^{m}(j) can be expressed as (Notation 3.4)

σ=ρ(1)​ω(1)​ρ(2)​ω(2)​…​ρ(j)​ω(j)​ρ(j+1),\sigma=\rho^{(1)}\omega^{(1)}\rho^{(2)}\omega^{(2)}\ldots\rho^{(j)}\omega^{(j)}\rho^{(j+1)},

where for all i∈[j+1]i\in[j+1], ρ(i)∼𝐩\rho^{(i)}\sim\mathbf{p}.

Let τ\tau be a permutation of length K−2​m=|𝐰|K-2m=|\mathbf{w}|. Permuting each ω(i)\omega^{(i)} by τ\tau and letting 𝐰′\mathbf{w}^{\prime} be 𝐰\mathbf{w} permuted by τ\tau, we get a permutation σ′\sigma^{\prime} that is covered by π′=𝐩𝐰′​𝐬\pi^{\prime}=\mathbf{p}\mathbf{w}^{\prime}\mathbf{s} with overlaps mm. This process is clearly reversible, which proves the claim. ∎

Example 3.7.

In the first column of Table 1 we see that 1-packings (overlap m=1m=1) of all the 5-patterns with π1=1\pi_{1}=1 and π5=4\pi_{5}=4 have the same enumeration.

In the following lemma, an nn-permutation is a permutation of {1,2,…,n}\{1,2,\ldots,n\}.

Lemma 3.8.

Let π=𝐩𝐰𝐬\pi=\mathbf{p}\mathbf{w}\mathbf{s} be a KK-pattern whose mm-prefix 𝐩\mathbf{p} and mm-suffix 𝐬\mathbf{s} are order isomorphic, m≤K/2m\leq K/2 and 𝐰\mathbf{w} is any permutation of the remaining letters. Let 𝐩′\mathbf{p}^{\prime} and 𝐬′\mathbf{s}^{\prime} be 𝐩\mathbf{p} and 𝐬\mathbf{s} permuted by the same permutation τ\tau and let 𝐰′\mathbf{w}^{\prime} be 𝐰\mathbf{w} permuted by some permutation ρ.\rho. Then the number of nn-permutations covered by π\pi with overlaps mm equals the number of nn-permutations covered by π′=𝐩′​𝐰′​𝐬′\pi^{\prime}=\mathbf{p}^{\prime}\mathbf{w}^{\prime}\mathbf{s}^{\prime} with overlaps mm.

Proof.

Given a permutation σ\sigma mm-covered by π\pi, permute by τ\tau the letters corresponding to 𝐩\mathbf{p} and 𝐬\mathbf{s}, respectively, in every occurrence of π\pi in σ\sigma, and permute by ρ\rho the letters between these occurrences of 𝐩\mathbf{p}/𝐬\mathbf{s}, that is, the letters of the ω(i)\omega^{(i)} in Notation 3.4. This turns every occurrence of π\pi into an occurrence of π′\pi^{\prime}, and this is clearly reversible, so that the map thus defined is a bijection. ∎

Lemma 3.10.

Let π=𝐩𝐰𝐬\pi=\mathbf{p}\mathbf{w}\mathbf{s} be a KK-pattern with mm-prefix 𝐩\mathbf{p} and mm-suffix 𝐬\mathbf{s} where m≤K/2m\leq K/2. The number of permutations mm-packing jj occurrences of π\pi equals the number of permutations mm-packing jj occurrences of π′=𝐬𝐰𝐩\pi^{\prime}=\mathbf{s}\mathbf{w}\mathbf{p}.

Proof.

By reversing each of 𝐩,𝐰\mathbf{p},\mathbf{w} and 𝐬\mathbf{s} and then reversing the resulting word, we obtain π′\pi^{\prime}, and by Lemmas 3.2 and 3.8 this does not affect the enumeration of permutations mm-packing π\pi. ∎

Referring to the second column of Table 1, 2-packing the pattern 1342513425 gives the same enumeration as 2-packing 2541325413.

Remark 3.12.

By Lemma 3.8, when m≤K/2m\leq K/2 and 𝐩∼𝐬\mathbf{p}\sim\mathbf{s}, we may sort the prefix, the suffix, and the letters between them, respectively, to increasing order without affecting the enumeration of permutations covered by π\pi for a given overlap. Without affecting the enumeration, we may also swap the prefix and suffix, by Lemma 3.10, and also apply any of the symmetries in Lemma 3.2. In what follows most of the examples and results we give for particular patterns or families of patterns consist of the canonical representative of each equivalence class with respect to these symmetries, which is the lexicographically least pattern in the class. As an example, the canonical representative of the class containing 37461285, for overlap 3, is 14738256, obtained by taking the reverse complement 41783526 of 37461285 and then sorting each of 417, 83 and 526 to increasing order. This is equivalent to first switching prefix and suffix, then taking complement and finally sorting each of the three parts.

Definition 3.13.

The content of a word w=a1​a2​…​anw=a_{1}a_{2}\ldots a_{n} is the set {a1,a2,…,an}\{a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{n}\}.

Lemma 3.14.

Suppose π\pi and π′\pi^{\prime} are two KK-patterns, each having mm-prefix isomorphic to its mm-suffix where K/2<m≤2​K/3K/2<m\leq 2K/3. If the mm-prefixes of π\pi and π′\pi^{\prime} have the same content, and likewise their mm-suffixes, then π\pi and π′\pi^{\prime} have the same enumeration.

Proof.

Since m>K/2m>K/2, the mm-prefix 𝐩\mathbf{p} and mm-suffix 𝐬\mathbf{s} of π\pi intersect in ℓ=2​m−K\ell=2m-K letters, and likewise for π′\pi^{\prime}. We denote the word consisting of this intersection by πx\pi_{x}, respectively πx′\pi^{\prime}_{x}. The content of πx\pi_{x} and πx′\pi^{\prime}_{x} must be the same since the prefixes of π\pi and π′\pi^{\prime} have the same content and their suffixes have the same content, respectively.

Let π=πi​πa​πx​πb​πf\pi=\pi_{i}\pi_{a}\pi_{x}\pi_{b}\pi_{f}, where πi,πx\pi_{i},\pi_{x} and πf\pi_{f} each have length ℓ=2​m−K\ell=2m-K, so πa\pi_{a} and πb\pi_{b} each have length m−2​ℓm-2\ell, and define πi′\pi^{\prime}_{i} etc. analogously. Thus, 𝐩=πi​πa​πx\mathbf{p}=\pi_{i}\pi_{a}\pi_{x} and 𝐬=πx​πb​πf\mathbf{s}=\pi_{x}\pi_{b}\pi_{f}, and therefore, since 𝐩\mathbf{p} and 𝐬\mathbf{s} are order isomorphic, πi,πx\pi_{i},\pi_{x} and πf\pi_{f} must all be order isomorphic, and πa\pi_{a} and πb\pi_{b} must be order isomorphic, and likewise for π′\pi^{\prime}. Note that if m=2​K/3m=2K/3 (so 3​ℓ=K3\ell=K) then πa\pi_{a} and πb\pi_{b} are empty, but this does not affect the following argument.

We now show that given the content of 𝐩\mathbf{p} and 𝐬\mathbf{s} the content of πx\pi_{x} determines the content of each of πi,πa,πb,πf\pi_{i},\pi_{a},\pi_{b},\pi_{f}: Since 𝐩\mathbf{p} and 𝐬\mathbf{s} are order isomorphic, the letters of πx\pi_{x} stand in the same relation in terms of size to the letters of the word πb​πf\pi_{b}\pi_{f} as πi\pi_{i} does to the letters of the word πa​πx\pi_{a}\pi_{x}. As an example, if the letters of πx\pi_{x} were the second, fifth and sixth in size among the letters of πx​πb​πf\pi_{x}\pi_{b}\pi_{f}, then the letters of πi\pi_{i} must be the second, fifth and sixth in size among the letters of πi​πa​πx\pi_{i}\pi_{a}\pi_{x}. Thus, the content of πx\pi_{x} determines the content of πi\pi_{i} and, analogously, the content of πf\pi_{f}. The remaining letters of 𝐩\mathbf{p} are just πa\pi_{a}, whose content is thus also determined, and likewise for πb\pi_{b}.

Since the content of πx\pi_{x} equals that of πx′\pi^{\prime}_{x}, the argument in the preceding paragraph implies that πi\pi_{i} and πi′\pi^{\prime}_{i} must have the same content, and likewise for πf,πf′\pi_{f},\pi^{\prime}_{f} and thus also πa,πa′\pi_{a},\pi^{\prime}_{a} and πb,πb′\pi_{b},\pi^{\prime}_{b}.

Now, πi,πx,πf\pi_{i},\pi_{x},\pi_{f} are order isomorphic and πa,πb\pi_{a},\pi_{b} are order isomorphic, and likewise for π′\pi^{\prime}. There is thus a permutation τ\tau that takes πi,πx\pi_{i},\pi_{x} and πf\pi_{f} to πi′,πx′\pi^{\prime}_{i},\pi^{\prime}_{x} and πf′\pi^{\prime}_{f}, respectively, and a permutation ρ\rho that takes πa\pi_{a} to πa′\pi^{\prime}_{a} and πb\pi_{b} to πb′\pi^{\prime}_{b}. Given a permutation covered by π\pi with overlaps mm we can split it into segments corresponding to πi,πa,πx,πb,πf​…\pi_{i},\pi_{a},\pi_{x},\pi_{b},\pi_{f}\ldots. Permuting each segment corresponding to πi,πx\pi_{i},\pi_{x} or πf\pi_{f} by τ\tau and each segment corresponding to πa\pi_{a} or πb\pi_{b} by ρ\rho we get a permutation covered by π′\pi^{\prime} with overlaps mm. Since this is clearly reversible it constitutes a bijection proving the lemma. ∎

The following lemma follows from the proof of Lemma 3.14.

Lemma 3.15.

Given a pattern π\pi with πi,πa,πx,πb,πf\pi_{i},\pi_{a},\pi_{x},\pi_{b},\pi_{f} as in Lemma 3.14 and K/2<m≤2​K/3K/2<m\leq 2K/3, let π′\pi^{\prime} be the pattern obtained from π\pi by permuting all of πi,πx,πf\pi_{i},\pi_{x},\pi_{f} by an arbitrary permutation τ\tau and permuting both πa\pi_{a} and πb\pi_{b} by an arbitrary permutation ρ\rho. Then π\pi and π′\pi^{\prime} have the same enumeration with respect to overlap mm.

As an example, for overlap 5 the patterns 13725846 and 31752864 have the same enumeration, since their prefixes and suffixes have content {1,2,3,5,7}\{1,2,3,5,7\} and {2,4,5,6,8}\{2,4,5,6,8\}, respectively.

Remark 3.16.

For m≤K/2m\leq K/2, Lemma 3.8 is analogous to Lemma 3.14. In the former case, however, there are no restrictions on how we may permute the prefix/suffix, as they don’t intersect.

Note that Table 1 also contains examples of patterns π\pi and π′\pi^{\prime} (such as 2143 and 2413) that have the same size and identical numbers of 11-packings, but different numbers of 22-packings.

Important convention: For a KK-pattern, the overlap mm is always taken to satisfy 1≤m<K1\leq m<K. For m≤K/2m\leq K/2, we will generally take the mm-prefix 𝐩\mathbf{p} and mm-suffix 𝐬\mathbf{s} to be increasing and 𝐩1<𝐬1\mathbf{p}_{1}<\mathbf{s}_{1}, since any pattern can be transformed to adhere to that without affecting its enumerative properties. For a KK-pattern with m>K/2m>K/2, we will generally assume that 11 does not belong to the suffix, which can be accomplished by reversal if need be, since 11 can not belong to the intersection of 𝐩\mathbf{p} and 𝐬\mathbf{s} as we shall later show. We also always assume that, given a KK-pattern π\pi and overlap mm, 𝐩\mathbf{p} and 𝐬\mathbf{s} are order isomorphic, since otherwise there are no permutations (m,j)(m,j)-covered by π\pi for j>1j>1.

In the study of permutation patterns, two patterns π\pi and π′\pi^{\prime} are said to be Wilf equivalent if the permutations avoiding π\pi are equinumerous with the permutations avoiding π′\pi^{\prime}. (A stronger notion of equivalence is achieved by not only considering avoidance, but any given number of occurrences.) In our context we declare two pairs (π,m)(\pi,m) and (π′,m′)(\pi^{\prime},m^{\prime}) to be Wilf equivalent if 𝒮πm​(j)\mathcal{S}_{\pi}^{m}(j) and 𝒮π′m′​(j)\mathcal{S}_{\pi^{\prime}}^{m^{\prime}}(j) have the same size for all jj. Of course, the numerical equivalences presented in the symmetry lemmas in this section all imply Wilf equivalence, but it seems there are many other Wilf equivalences, even for patterns and overlaps of different lengths, and we mention some of these in Section 7.

4 Generating function and general recurrence

In this section, we establish two general enumeration results: an explicit rational multivariate generating function for 11-packings of an arbitrary pattern, and a recurrence for mm-packings when m≤K/2m\leq K/2.

4.1 A rational generating function for 11-packings

At first sight, the enumeration of 11-packings appears to depend rather sensitively on the pattern (cf. Table 1). Surprisingly, however, despite the variety of packing sequences that arise in subsequent sections, all overlap-11 counts admit a single multivariate generating function formula.

For j≥1j\geq 1, let x1,…,xj,y1,…,yj,z1,…,zjx_{1},\ldots,x_{j},y_{1},\ldots,y_{j},z_{1},\ldots,z_{j} be commuting indeterminates and work in the formal power series ring

ℤ⁡[[x1,…,xj,y1,…,yj,z1,…,zj]].\mathbb{Z}[[x_{1},\ldots,x_{j},y_{1},\ldots,y_{j},z_{1},\ldots,z_{j}]].

Write

𝐱=(x1,…,xj),𝐲=(y1,…,yj),𝐳=(z1,…,zj),\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{j}),\qquad\mathbf{y}=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{j}),\qquad\mathbf{z}=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{j}),

and set

B0:=∑r=1jxr,Bi:=∑r=1i−1zr+yi+∑r=i+1jxr,1≤i≤j,Bj+1:=∑r=1jzr,B_{0}:=\sum_{r=1}^{j}x_{r},\quad\quad B_{i}:=\sum_{r=1}^{i-1}z_{r}+y_{i}+\sum_{r=i+1}^{j}x_{r},\qquad 1\leq i\leq j,\quad\quad B_{j+1}:=\sum_{r=1}^{j}z_{r},

where an empty sum is understood to be zero. Furthermore, for a∈ℤ≥0a\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}, denote

𝐱ja:=(∏i=1jxi)a,𝐲ja:=(∏i=1jyi)a,𝐳ja:=(∏i=1jzi)a,\mathbf{x}_{j}^{a}:=\left(\prod_{i=1}^{j}x_{i}\right)^{a},\qquad\mathbf{y}_{j}^{a}:=\left(\prod_{i=1}^{j}y_{i}\right)^{a},\qquad\mathbf{z}_{j}^{a}:=\left(\prod_{i=1}^{j}z_{i}\right)^{a},

with zeroth powers equal to 11, the multiplicative identity in the ring of formal power series.

Theorem 4.1.

Let π\pi be a KK-pattern with π1<πK\pi_{1}<\pi_{K}. The number of permutations 11-packing jj occurrences of π\pi is the coefficient of

𝐱jπ1−1​𝐲jπK−π1−1​𝐳jK−πK\mathbf{x}_{j}^{\pi_{1}-1}\mathbf{y}_{j}^{\pi_{K}-\pi_{1}-1}\mathbf{z}_{j}^{K-\pi_{K}}

in the formal power series

Fj​(𝐱,𝐲,𝐳):=∏i=0j+111−Bi.F_{j}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y},\mathbf{z}):=\prod_{i=0}^{j+1}\frac{1}{1-B_{i}}. (4.1)

Expanding the notation we have the following expression: 11 1 Note that setting xi=yi=zi=0x_{i}=y_{i}=z_{i}=0 when i<1i<1 or i>ji>j, Equation (4.2) simplifies to this: Fj​(𝐱,𝐲,𝐳)=1∏i=0j+1(1−(∑r=1i−1zr+yi+∑r=i+1jxr)).F_{j}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y},\mathbf{z})=\dfrac{1}{\displaystyle\prod_{i=0}^{j+1}\left(1-\left(\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{i-1}z_{r}+y_{i}+\displaystyle\sum_{r=i+1}^{j}x_{r}\right)\right)}.

Fj​(𝐱,𝐲,𝐳)=1(1−∑r=1jxr)​∏i=1j(1−(∑r=1i−1zr+yi+∑r=i+1jxr))​(1−∑r=1jzr).F_{j}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y},\mathbf{z})=\dfrac{1}{\left(1-\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{j}x_{r}\right)\displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^{j}\left(1-\left(\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{i-1}z_{r}+y_{i}+\displaystyle\sum_{r=i+1}^{j}x_{r}\right)\right)\left(1-\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{j}z_{r}\right)}. (4.2)

Therefore, for 22 occurrences, we look for the coefficient of

(x1​x2)π1−1​(y1​y2)πK−π1−1​(z1​z2)K−πK(x_{1}x_{2})^{\pi_{1}-1}(y_{1}y_{2})^{\pi_{K}-\pi_{1}-1}(z_{1}z_{2})^{K-\pi_{K}}

in

1(1−(x1+x2))​(1−(y1+x2))​(1−(z1+y2))​(1−(z1+z2)).\dfrac{1}{(1-(x_{1}+x_{2}))(1-(y_{1}+x_{2}))(1-(z_{1}+y_{2}))(1-(z_{1}+z_{2}))}. (4.3)

For 33 occurrences, we look for the coefficient of

(x1​x2​x3)π1−1​(y1​y2​y3)πK−π1−1​(z1​z2​z3)K−πK(x_{1}x_{2}x_{3})^{\pi_{1}-1}(y_{1}y_{2}y_{3})^{\pi_{K}-\pi_{1}-1}(z_{1}z_{2}z_{3})^{K-\pi_{K}}

×1(1−z1−z2−y3)​(1−z1−z2−z3).\displaystyle\times\frac{1}{(1-z_{1}-z_{2}-y_{3})(1-z_{1}-z_{2}-z_{3})}.
Corollary 4.3.

The number of permutations 11-packing 22 occurrences of a KK-pattern π\pi is

(π1+πK−2πK−1)​(2​K−π1−πKK−πK).\binom{\pi_{1}+\pi_{K}-2}{\pi_{K}-1}\binom{2K-\pi_{1}-\pi_{K}}{K-\pi_{K}}.
Proof.

By complementation, we may assume π1<πK\pi_{1}<\pi_{K}. Set

a=π1−1,b=πK−π1−1,c=K−πK.a=\pi_{1}-1,\qquad b=\pi_{K}-\pi_{1}-1,\qquad c=K-\pi_{K}.

in (4.3) gives the product

(∑r=0a(a+ra)​(a+b−rb))​(∑s=0c(b+sb)​(2​c−sc)).\left(\sum_{r=0}^{a}\binom{a+r}{a}\binom{a+b-r}{b}\right)\left(\sum_{s=0}^{c}\binom{b+s}{b}\binom{2c-s}{c}\right).

∑r=0n(p+rp)​(q+n−rq)=(p+q+n+1n),\sum_{r=0}^{n}\binom{p+r}{p}\binom{q+n-r}{q}=\binom{p+q+n+1}{n},

which gives the stated expression. ∎

Prior to proving the main theorem of this section, we introduce some additional notation. Fix j,K∈ℕj,K\in\mathbb{N} and, for each i∈[j]i\in[j], denote by IiI_{i} the set of positions occupied by the iith prescribed occurrence of π\pi in a permutation that 11-packs jj occurrences, i.e.

Ii:={1+(i−1)​(K−1),…,K+(i−1)​(K−1)}.I_{i}:=\{1+(i-1)(K-1),\ldots,K+(i-1)(K-1)\}.

ei:=1+i⁡(K−1).e_{i}:=1+i(K-1).

Then eie_{i} is the unique element of Ii∩Ii+1I_{i}\cap I_{i+1} for 1≤i≤j−11\leq i\leq j-1, while e0e_{0} and eje_{j} are the first and last positions of the packing, respectively. For i∈[j]i\in[j], we call ei−1e_{i-1} and eie_{i} the boundary positions of the iith occurrence and set

Accordingly, we refer to σ⁡(ei−1)\sigma(e_{i-1}) and σ⁡(ei)\sigma(e_{i}) as boundary values. Viewing σ\sigma as a map [j​K−(j−1)]→[j​K−(j−1)][jK-(j-1)]\to[jK-(j-1)], the occurrences of π\pi naturally partition the domain of σ\sigma into the blocks

{e0},I^1,{e1},I^2,…,{ej−1},I^j,{ej}.\{e_{0}\},\widehat{I}_{1},\{e_{1}\},\widehat{I}_{2},\ldots,\{e_{j-1}\},\widehat{I}_{j},\{e_{j}\}.

In the following, we once again denote by 𝒮π1​(j)\mathcal{S}_{\pi}^{1}(j) the set of permutations in 𝒮j​K−j+1\mathcal{S}_{jK-j+1} 11-packing jj occurrences of a KK-pattern π\pi.

We now state an elementary lemma concerning 11-packings of a pattern π\pi that will be used in the construction below.

Lemma 4.4.

Consider a permutation σ∈𝒮n\sigma\in\mathcal{S}_{n} with an occurrence of a KK-pattern π\pi spanning a set of consecutive indices A={a,…,a+K−1}A=\{a,\ldots,a+K-1\}. Let A^:={a+1,…,a+K−2}\widehat{A}:=\{a+1,\ldots,a+K-2\}. Assume π1<πK\pi_{1}<\pi_{K}. Then there are exactly π1−1\pi_{1}-1 indices k∈A^k\in\widehat{A} such that σ⁡(k)<σ⁡(a)\sigma(k)<\sigma(a), exactly πK−π1−1\pi_{K}-\pi_{1}-1 indices such that σ⁡(a)<σ⁡(k)<σ⁡(a+K−1)\sigma(a)<\sigma(k)<\sigma(a+K-1), and exactly K−πKK-\pi_{K} indices such that σ⁡(k)>σ⁡(a+K−1)\sigma(k)>\sigma(a+K-1).

Proof.

Immediate from the relative order prescribed by π\pi. ∎

Definition 4.5.

Given a KK-pattern π\pi with π1<πK\pi_{1}<\pi_{K} and j∈ℕj\in\mathbb{N}, let 𝒲1,π,j\mathcal{W}_{1,\pi,j} denote the set of words of length j​K−j+1jK-j+1 on the alphabet

𝒜j:={x1,…,xj,y1,…,yj,z1,…,zj,w0,w1,…,wj}\mathcal{A}_{j}:=\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{j},y_{1},\ldots,y_{j},z_{1},\ldots,z_{j},w_{0},w_{1},\ldots,w_{j}\}

satisfying the following conditions:

  1. A1.

    Each element of {w0,w1,…,wj}\{w_{0},w_{1},\ldots,w_{j}\} appears exactly once, and these elements appear in increasing order of their indices.

  2. A2.

    Every place to the left of w0w_{0} is occupied by a letter in {x1,…,xj}\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{j}\}.

  3. A3.

    Every place to the right of wjw_{j} is occupied by a letter in {z1,…,zj}\{z_{1},\ldots,z_{j}\}.

  4. A4.

4.2 General recurrence

We now give a recursive formula for computing the number of permutations of a given length that are covered by a given KK-pattern with overlaps m≤K/2m\leq K/2. For simplicity we assume the mm-prefix, and thus the mm-suffix, of the pattern in question to be increasing, as Lemma 3.8 shows that the theorem also applies if we permute the prefix and suffix in the same way. The following remark explains the treatment of separated components.

The following theorem first appeared in the authors’ extended abstract for the fpsac-conference 2023 [1]. For m=1m=1, the corresponding recurrence, with the first rather than the last boundary value recorded, appears as (8) in the proof of Theorem 28 in [3]. Their statement concerns patterns whose distinct occurrences cannot overlap in more than one position. Here only the prescribed overlaps have size one; additional occurrences are allowed.

Theorem 4.7.

Let m≤K/2m\leq K/2 and let π\pi be a KK-pattern with mm-prefix 𝐩\mathbf{p} and mm-suffix 𝐬\mathbf{s}, where 𝐩\mathbf{p} and 𝐬\mathbf{s} are increasing and 𝐩1<𝐬1\mathbf{p}_{1}<\mathbf{s}_{1}. Put nj=K+j⁡(K−m)n_{j}=K+j(K-m) for j≥0j\geq 0.

Then g0​(𝐬)=1g_{0}(\mathbf{s})=1, g0​(L)=0g_{0}(L)=0 if L≠𝐬L\neq\mathbf{s}, and for j≥1j\geq 1 we have

gj​(L)=∑(ℓ1,…,ℓm)∈𝒜j​(L)gj−1​(ℓ1′,…,ℓm′)​∏i=02​m(ℓτi+1−ℓτi−1uτi+1−uτi−1),g_{j}(L)=\sum_{(\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{m})\in\mathcal{A}_{j}(L)}g_{j-1}(\ell^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,\ell^{\prime}_{m})\prod_{i=0}^{2m}\binom{\ell_{\tau_{i+1}}-\ell_{\tau_{i}}-1}{u_{\tau_{i+1}}-u_{\tau_{i}}-1}, (4.5)

where ℓi′=ℓi−(ui−i)\ell^{\prime}_{i}=\ell_{i}-(u_{i}-i) for 1≤i≤m1\leq i\leq m, and 𝒜j​(L)\mathcal{A}_{j}(L) is the set of sequences {(ℓ1,…,ℓm)\{(\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{m}) satisfying

0<ℓτ1<⋯<ℓτ2​m<nj+1}.0<\ell_{\tau_{1}}<\cdots<\ell_{\tau_{2m}}<n_{j}+1\}.

In the product, ℓ0=0\ell_{0}=0 and ℓ2​m+1=nj+1\ell_{2m+1}=n_{j}+1. Here (uv)=0\binom{u}{v}=0 if u<vu<v.

Consequently, the number hj=|𝒮πm​(j+1)|h_{j}=|\mathcal{S}_{\pi}^{m}(j+1)| of such packings is

hj=∑1≤ℓm+1<⋯<ℓ2​m≤njgj​(ℓm+1,…,ℓ2​m).h_{j}=\sum_{1\leq\ell_{m+1}<\cdots<\ell_{2m}\leq n_{j}}g_{j}(\ell_{m+1},\ldots,\ell_{2m}). (4.6)
Proof.

We prove this by induction on jj, the base case, when j=0j=0, being g0​(L)=1g_{0}(L)=1 if and only if L=𝐬L=\mathbf{s}, since there is precisely one permutation of size KK with an occurrence of the pattern π\pi, namely the permutation consisting of π\pi itself.

In order to construct a permutation of size njn_{j} covered by π\pi with overlaps mm and ending with L=ℓm+1​ℓm+2​…​ℓ2​mL=\ell_{m+1}\ell_{m+2}\ldots\ell_{2m}, let 𝒪=𝒪F​𝒪M​𝒪L\mathcal{O}=\mathcal{O}_{F}\mathcal{O}_{M}\mathcal{O}_{L} be the word consisting of the last occurrence of π\pi in such a permutation σ\sigma, and such that both 𝒪F\mathcal{O}_{F} and 𝒪L\mathcal{O}_{L} have length mm. Thus 𝒪F=ℓ1⋯ℓm\mathcal{O}_{F}=\ell_{1}\cdots\ell_{m} and 𝒪L=L\mathcal{O}_{L}=L, and (ℓ1,…,ℓm)∈𝒜j​(L)(\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{m})\in\mathcal{A}_{j}(L). We first analyze the possible choices of letters in σ\sigma that constitute 𝒪M\mathcal{O}_{M}.

Let a<ba<b be two letters in 𝒪\mathcal{O} that belong to the union of 𝒪F\mathcal{O}_{F} and 𝒪L\mathcal{O}_{L} and such that no letter cc in 𝒪F\mathcal{O}_{F} or 𝒪L\mathcal{O}_{L} satisfies a<c<ba<c<b. Thus, a=ℓτia=\ell_{\tau_{i}} and b=ℓτi+1b=\ell_{\tau_{i+1}} for some ii, where τ\tau is the permutation defined in the statement of the theorem. However, there may be letters in 𝒪M\mathcal{O}_{M} that lie between aa and bb in size. In fact, there must be precisely uτi+1−uτi−1u_{\tau_{i+1}}-u_{\tau_{i}}-1 such letters in 𝒪M\mathcal{O}_{M}, in order for 𝒪\mathcal{O} to be an occurrence of π\pi. Moreover, these letters can be any of those that lie strictly between ℓτi\ell_{\tau_{i}} and ℓτi+1\ell_{\tau_{i+1}} in size. In addition, there may be letters in 𝒪M\mathcal{O}_{M} that are smaller or greater than all letters in 𝒪F\mathcal{O}_{F} and 𝒪L\mathcal{O}_{L}, which is taken care of by the definitions of τ0,τ2​m+1\tau_{0},\tau_{2m+1} etc. There are therefore (ℓτi+1−ℓτi−1uτi+1−uτi−1)\binom{\ell_{\tau_{i+1}}-\ell_{\tau_{i}}-1}{u_{\tau_{i+1}}-u_{\tau_{i}}-1} possible choices for these letters in 𝒪M\mathcal{O}_{M}. Having thus chosen the letters to form 𝒪M\mathcal{O}_{M} there is only one way to order them so that they will form the part of an occurrence of π\pi that lies between the mm-prefix and the mm-suffix of that occurrence.

In order to complete the desired permutation σ\sigma, we must construct a word σ′\sigma^{\prime} of size nj−1n_{j-1}, with π\pi-overlaps mm, and ending in ℓ1,…,ℓm\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{m}. Its alphabet is the set RR obtained from [nj][n_{j}] by removing the letters of 𝒪M\mathcal{O}_{M} and 𝒪L\mathcal{O}_{L}. This leaves nj−1n_{j-1} letters, including all of 𝒪F\mathcal{O}_{F}.

To do so, we define σ′′\sigma^{\prime\prime} as the permutation of [nj−1][n_{j-1}] order isomorphic to σ′\sigma^{\prime}. Standardization preserves every prescribed occurrence. σ′′\sigma^{\prime\prime} has a suffix ℓ1−(u1−1)​…​ℓm−(um−m)\ell_{1}-(u_{1}-1)\ldots\ell_{m}-(u_{m}-m) because among the ui−1u_{i}-1 letters of 𝒪\mathcal{O} smaller than ℓi\ell_{i}, exactly i−1i-1 belong to the increasing prefix 𝒪F\mathcal{O}_{F}. Hence there are exactly ui−iu_{i}-i letters in 𝒪M\mathcal{O}_{M} and 𝒪L\mathcal{O}_{L} smaller than ℓi\ell_{i}. By the inductive hypothesis, there are precisely gj−1​(ℓ1−(u1−1),…,ℓm−(um−m))g_{j-1}(\ell_{1}-(u_{1}-1),\ldots,\ell_{m}-(u_{m}-m)) such σ′′\sigma^{\prime\prime}.

Each such σ′′\sigma^{\prime\prime} uniquely determines σ′\sigma^{\prime} on the alphabet RR, and appending 𝒪M​𝒪L\mathcal{O}_{M}\mathcal{O}_{L} gives the required packing. Conversely, the packing uniquely determines all these choices. Since the choices in the disjoint intervals are independent, their numbers multiply. Summing gives (4.5), and (4.6) follows by partitioning packings according to their final mm letters. ∎

Remark 4.8 (Separated components).

In cases where not all pairs of successive prescribed occurrences are required to overlap, this breaks the problem into smaller pieces of overlapping occurrences — whose enumeration can be computed via Theorem 4.7 — and segments of letters in a permutation that are not required to belong to an occurrence. We then need to multiply by the appropriate multinomial coefficient, corresponding to choices of letters for each piece, and the appropriate factorial for the letters not required to belong to an occurrence, since those letters can be ordered arbitrarily.

The procedure of Theorem 4.7 is computationally efficient, in the sense that for a fixed KK-pattern and a fixed mm, hjh_{j} can be computed in time polynomial in jj. However, for j>1j>1, the methods developed in the next section, turning this computation into counting linear extensions of posets, are more efficient in our implementations.

5 Pattern-packing posets

In Table 1 we presented enumerative results for a few patterns whose enumeration by combinatorial arguments is fairly simple in the cases where we have explicit formulas, all of which are presented in greater generality later in this section. For most patterns, however, computing the enumeration is far from straightforward, as they translate to very different combinatorial problems, requiring distinct arguments and often diverse techniques. Different patterns also pose vastly different levels of challenge. While the explicit results in Table 1 are low-hanging fruit, the other sequences, apart from 14325 with overlap 2, were not known at the time of initiating this study (at least not found in the OEIS [14]), and that is the case for the vast majority of sequences we have encountered.

In this section we show that the permutations (m,j)(m,j)-packing a pattern π\pi are in one-to-one correspondence with the linear extensions of a poset determined by π\pi, mm and jj, where the poset for jj is an induced subposet of the one for j+1j+1. A linear extension of a poset 𝒫\mathcal{P} is a total ordering 𝒪\mathcal{O} of its elements so that if x<yx<y in 𝒫\mathcal{P} then xx precedes yy in 𝒪\mathcal{O}.

This correspondence was previously described for certain classes of patterns by Dotsenko and Khoroshkin [3] and by Elizalde and Noy [8] and used to derive generating functions counting packings of certain patterns. Here we elicit several general structural properties of these posets and characterize completely those patterns the Hasse diagrams of whose posets are trees or, in particular, chains (total orders). These structural properties in many cases suggest effective techniques for enumerating linear extensions, which often explains why permutations covered by different patterns have the same enumeration.

We begin by observing that the act of packing a given number of occurrences of a consecutive permutation pattern π\pi forces relations between the elements of the permutation thus covered by π\pi. For example, recalling Definition 2.2 of the order isomorphism of permutations, any permutation σ\sigma 1-packing two occurrences of π=2413\pi=2413 must simultaneously satisfy:

σ1σ2σ3σ4∼π,which is equivalent toσ3<σ1<σ4<σ2(first occurrence)\sigma_{1}\,\sigma_{2}\,\sigma_{3}\,\sigma_{4}\sim\pi,~\mbox{which is equivalent to}~~\sigma_{3}<\sigma_{1}<\sigma_{4}<\sigma_{2}~\mbox{(first occurrence)}

and also

σ4σ5σ6σ7∼π,which is equivalent to σ6<σ4<σ7<σ5(second occurrence).\sigma_{4}\,\sigma_{5}\,\sigma_{6}\,\sigma_{7}\sim\pi,~~\mbox{which is equivalent to }~\sigma_{6}<\sigma_{4}<\sigma_{7}<\sigma_{5}~\mbox{(second occurrence)}.

This implies, for example, that σ2\sigma_{2} must be greater than σ6\sigma_{6}, because σ6<σ4<σ2\sigma_{6}<\sigma_{4}<\sigma_{2}.

As before, let 𝒮πm​(j)\mathcal{S}_{\pi}^{m}(j) denote the set of permutations mm-packing jj occurrences of a KK-pattern π\pi. Given π\pi, any permutation σ∈𝒮πm​(j)\sigma\in\mathcal{S}_{\pi}^{m}(j) (trivially) satisfies the following equivalences, where d=K−md=K-m:

σ1​…​σK∼π\displaystyle\sigma_{1}\,\ldots\,\sigma_{K}\sim\pi
σ1+d​…​σK+d∼π\displaystyle\sigma_{1+d}\,\ldots\,\sigma_{K+d}\sim\pi
⋮\displaystyle~~~~~~~~~~~~~\vdots
σ1+(j−1)​d​…​σK+(j−1)​d∼π.\displaystyle\sigma_{1+(j-1)d}\ldots\sigma_{K+(j-1)d}\sim\pi.

These statements are straightforwardly seen to correspond to the following inequalities.

Lemma 5.1.

A permutation σ\sigma (m,j)(m,j)-packs a KK-pattern π\pi if and only if σ\sigma has length K+(j−1)​(K−m)K+(j-1)(K-m) and satisfies the following jj inequalities, where τ=π−1\tau=\pi^{-1} and d=K−md=K-m:

σ⁡(τ1)<σ⁡(τ2)<⋯<σ⁡(τK)\displaystyle\sigma(\tau_{1})<\sigma(\tau_{2})<\cdots<\sigma(\tau_{K})
σ⁡(τ1+d)<σ⁡(τ2+d)<⋯<σ⁡(τK+d)\displaystyle\sigma(\tau_{1}+d)<\sigma(\tau_{2}+d)<\cdots<\sigma(\tau_{K}+d)
⋮\displaystyle~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~\vdots (5.1)
σ⁡(τ1+(j−1)​d)<σ⁡(τ2+(j−1)​d)<⋯<σ⁡(τK+(j−1)​d)\displaystyle\sigma(\tau_{1}+(j-1)d)<\sigma(\tau_{2}+(j-1)d)<\cdots<\sigma(\tau_{K}+(j-1)d)
Definition 5.2 (Pattern-packing posets).

Given a KK-pattern π\pi, overlap mm and number of occurrences jj, the poset 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) defined by the inequalities (5.1) is said to be a pattern-packing poset, or just a pattern poset, for π\pi.

The relationship between pattern-packing permutations and pattern-packing posets follows immediately from Lemma 5.1:

Theorem 5.3.

Given a pattern π\pi, overlap mm and number of occurrences jj, the set of linear extensions of the poset 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) is in natural bijection with 𝒮πm​(j)\mathcal{S}_{\pi}^{m}(j).

More precisely, the inverses of the permutations (m,j)(m,j)-packing a pattern π\pi are exactly the linear extensions of the poset 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j).

In what follows, we will frequently refer to the sequence of inequalities in Lemma (5.1) as the jj-stack of 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j), which we now define. Given a KK-pattern π\pi and overlap mm, let τ\tau be the inverse, written in one-line notation, of π\pi (that is, if π\pi has jj in the ii-th place then τ\tau has ii in the jj-th place). For ℓ≥0\ell\geq 0, let

𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍ℓ=sℓ​1​sℓ​2​…​sℓ​K{\mathsf{shift}}_{\ell}=s_{\ell 1}s_{\ell 2}\ldots s_{\ell K} (5.2)

where sℓ​i=τi+ℓ⁡(K−m)s_{\ell i}=\tau_{i}+\ell(K-m). That is, 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0=τ{\mathsf{shift}}_{0}=\tau and, for ℓ>0\ell>0, 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍ℓ{\mathsf{shift}}_{\ell} is 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍ℓ−1{\mathsf{shift}}_{\ell-1} with each letter incremented by (K−m)(K-m). Generically, by Lemma 5.1, for any given KK-pattern π\pi and overlap mm, letting d=K−md=K-m we have:

𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0=τ1τ2τ3…τK𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍1=τ1+dτ2+dτ3+d…τK+d𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍2=τ1+2​dτ2+2​dτ3+2​d…τK+2​d⋮\begin{array}[]{ccccccccc}{\mathsf{shift}}_{0}&=&\tau_{1}&\tau_{2}&\tau_{3}&\ldots&\tau_{K}&\\ {\mathsf{shift}}_{1}&=&\tau_{1}+d&\tau_{2}+d&\tau_{3}+d&\ldots&\tau_{K}+d&\\ {\mathsf{shift}}_{2}&=&\tau_{1}+2d&\tau_{2}+2d&\tau_{3}+2d&\ldots&\tau_{K}+2d&\\ &\vdots\end{array} (5.3)
Definition 5.4.

We call the sequence 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0,𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍1,…,𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍j−1{\mathsf{shift}}_{0},{\mathsf{shift}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathsf{shift}}_{j-1} the jj-stack for 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) and refer to 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0,𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍1,…,𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍j−1{\mathsf{shift}}_{0},{\mathsf{shift}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathsf{shift}}_{j-1} as lines of the stack.

It follows that the poset 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) consists of the elements of the jj-stack for π\pi, with order generated by x<yx<y whenever xx appears before yy on some line. Here << denotes the poset order, not numerical order of the labels.

Example 5.5.

If π=143625\pi=143625, and overlap is m=2m=2, so d=4d=4, then τ=π−1=153264\tau=\pi^{-1}=153264, so

𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0=153264𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍1=5976108𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍2=91311101412\begin{array}[]{cccccccccc}{\mathsf{shift}}_{0}&=&1&5&3&2&6&4\\ {\mathsf{shift}}_{1}&=&5&9&7&6&10&8\\ {\mathsf{shift}}_{2}&=&9&13&11&10&14&12\end{array}

and the poset 𝒫π2​(3){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{2}(3) is pictured in Figure 5.1.

In Example 5.5, the letters 5 and 6 that appear in both 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0} and 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍1{\mathsf{shift}}_{1} (but not in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍2{\mathsf{shift}}_{2}) have different sets of letters between them in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0} and 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍1{\mathsf{shift}}_{1} (namely 3,23,2 and 9,79,7, respectively). This implies that the corresponding poset is not a total order. In fact, we will show (see Theorem 5.20) that this is enough to deduce that the poset is not a tree, when seen as the graph in Figure 5.1. The Hasse diagram of a poset 𝒫\mathcal{P} is a directed graph whose elements are the elements of 𝒫\mathcal{P} and where there is an edge from xx to yy if and only if xx is covered by yy, that is, x<yx<y and there is no zz so that x<z<yx<z<y. Instead of indicating the orientation of edges by arrows, a Hasse diagram is typically drawn so that an edge from xx to yy goes upwards from xx to yy. In Figure 5.1, 5 is covered by 3 and 9, and 6 covers 7 and 2, for example. Thus, the Hasse diagram of 𝒫πm​(ℓ){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(\ell) has vertices consisting of all the letters appearing in its ℓ\ell-stack, and the edges x→yx\rightarrow y if xx is covered by yy. Note, however, that although xx must immediately precede yy on some line of the stack in order to be covered by yy, this is not sufficient, since on a different line of the stack we may have a letter zz between xx and yy, as in Figure 5.3, where 5 immediately precedes 6 and 7, respectively, but 6 does not cover 5. We state a couple of observations on the structure of a stack. First, the letters from the first line that are repeated on the second line will necessarily be the mm largest letters of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0} and the mm smallest letters of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍1{\mathsf{shift}}_{1}, namely K−m+1,K−m+2,…,KK-m+1,K-m+2,\ldots,K. In 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0}, these appear in the places determined by the mm-suffix of π\pi (in the case of Figure 5.1 in places 2 and 5) and in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍1{\mathsf{shift}}_{1} they appear in the places determined by the mm-prefix of π\pi (places 1 and 4). Moreover, these repeated letters must appear in the same order in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0} and 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍1{\mathsf{shift}}_{1}, since their places are determined by the values, respectively, of the prefix and suffix of π\pi, which are order isomorphic (if they didn’t this would lead to a contradiction in the poset). This generalizes in the following obvious way:

Lemma 5.6.

Given a pattern π\pi and overlap mm, the letters appearing in both 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i{\mathsf{shift}}_{i} and 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i+1{\mathsf{shift}}_{i+1} are the mm largest letters of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i{\mathsf{shift}}_{i} and the mm smallest letters of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i+1{\mathsf{shift}}_{i+1}. Letters that belong to both 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i{\mathsf{shift}}_{i} and 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍ℓ{\mathsf{shift}}_{\ell}, for any ii and ℓ\ell, must appear in the same order in both.

The labels on 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i{\mathsf{shift}}_{i} form the integer interval [1+i​d,K+i​d][1+id,K+id]. Thus the lines containing a given label form an interval of line indices. Since incomparable elements cannot occur on the same line, we obtain:

Lemma 5.7.

If an element xx appears in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i{\mathsf{shift}}_{i} and 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍ℓ{\mathsf{shift}}_{\ell} where i<ℓi<\ell, then xx appears in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍k{\mathsf{shift}}_{k} for all kk with i<k<ℓi<k<\ell. In particular, if xx and yy are incomparable elements in 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) then either all lines in the stack for 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) containing xx must precede all lines containing yy, or vice versa.

The following lemma will be useful in a couple of places.

Lemma 5.8.

Given a KK-pattern π\pi and overlap mm, if m≤K/2m\leq K/2 then no letter will appear on more than two lines of the stack, and two lines with a common letter must be adjacent.

Proof.

The greatest letter of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i{\mathsf{shift}}_{i} is K+i⁡(K−m)K+i(K-m), which is smaller than the smallest letter of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i+2{\mathsf{shift}}_{i+2}, which is 1+(i+2)​(K−m)1+(i+2)(K-m). ∎

5.1 The general structure of pattern posets

The dual of a poset 𝒫\mathcal{P} is the poset with the same elements as 𝒫\mathcal{P} where y≤xy\leq x if and only if x≤yx\leq y in 𝒫\mathcal{P}. The Hasse diagram of the dual of 𝒫\mathcal{P} is obtained by turning the Hasse diagram of 𝒫\mathcal{P} upside down.

Remark 5.9.

It is straightforward to verify that apart from taking the complement of a pattern (dealt with in the following Lemma 5.10), the maps proving the lemmas about enumeration equivalences in Section 3 have corresponding maps on the posets for the patterns in question that give isomorphic posets, but with the labels of the elements permuted. As an example, to obtain the poset of the reverse of a pattern π\pi we complement its elements, that is, replace the largest label of an element in 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) with 1, the second largest with 2, and so on.

Lemma 5.10.

The dual of the pattern poset 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) is the pattern poset of the complement C⁡(π)C(\pi) of π\pi.

Proof.

The reverse of the inverse of a permutation π\pi is the inverse of the complement of π\pi. Thus, the inverses of π\pi and C⁡(π)C(\pi) are the reverses of each other. Therefore, each line of the stack for C⁡(π)C(\pi) is the reverse of the corresponding line of the stack for π\pi, which implies that the order relations of the posets (for a given number jj of occurrences) for π\pi and C⁡(π)C(\pi) are each other’s opposites. Therefore, these posets are each other’s duals. ∎

Theorem 5.11.

An element in 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) can cover at most two elements and can be covered by at most two elements.

Proof.

If an element xx in 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) is covered by yy, then yy must immediately follow xx in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i{\mathsf{shift}}_{i} for some ii. We then say that yy is a successor of xx (in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i{\mathsf{shift}}_{i}). In order for an element xx of 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) to be covered by three different elements in 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j), xx must have three different successors, in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍a,𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍b{\mathsf{shift}}_{a},{\mathsf{shift}}_{b} and 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍c{\mathsf{shift}}_{c}, respectively, for some a<b<ca<b<c. But since xx belongs to each of these shifts, every letter in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍b{\mathsf{shift}}_{b} that is smaller (in size) than xx must also belong to 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍a{\mathsf{shift}}_{a}, and every letter in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍b{\mathsf{shift}}_{b} that is greater than xx must also belong to 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍c{\mathsf{shift}}_{c}. In particular, the successor zz of xx in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍b{\mathsf{shift}}_{b} must also belong to either 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍a{\mathsf{shift}}_{a} or 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍c{\mathsf{shift}}_{c}. If zz also belongs to 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍a{\mathsf{shift}}_{a} then zz and the successor of xx in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍a{\mathsf{shift}}_{a} are comparable and so they can’t both cover xx in 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j). The case where zz belongs to 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍c{\mathsf{shift}}_{c} is analogous, and so no element of 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) can be covered by three different elements. Since the dual of a pattern poset is a pattern poset (Lemma 5.10), no letter can cover more than two letters. ∎

We now characterize the minimal and maximal elements of a pattern poset 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) based on whether 1 and KK belong to the prefix or suffix of π\pi (or neither).

Proposition 5.12.

Let π\pi be a KK-pattern with isomorphic mm-prefix 𝐩\mathbf{p} and mm-suffix 𝐬\mathbf{s}. Then the poset 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) satisfies the following:

  1. 1.

    If 𝐩\mathbf{p} contains 1 then the only minimal element of 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) is the first letter of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0}.

  2. 2.

    If 𝐬\mathbf{s} contains 1 then the only minimal element of 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) is the first letter of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍j−1{\mathsf{shift}}_{j-1}.

  3. 3.

    If 𝐩\mathbf{p} contains KK then the only maximal element of 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) is the last letter of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0}.

  4. 4.

    If 𝐬\mathbf{s} contains KK then the only maximal element of 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) is the last letter of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍j−1{\mathsf{shift}}_{j-1}.

  5. 5.

    If 1 belongs to neither 𝐩\mathbf{p} nor 𝐬\mathbf{s} then the first element of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i{\mathsf{shift}}_{i} for each ii is minimal in 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j).

  6. 6.

    If K belongs to neither 𝐩\mathbf{p} nor 𝐬\mathbf{s} then the last element of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i{\mathsf{shift}}_{i} for each ii is maximal in 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j).

It follows that, for j>1j>1, 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) has a single minimal element if and only if 1 belongs to either 𝐩\mathbf{p} or 𝐬\mathbf{s}, and a single maximal element if and only if KK belongs to either 𝐩\mathbf{p} or 𝐬\mathbf{s}.

Proof.

The only elements that can be minimal in the poset 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) are those appearing as the first letter of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i{\mathsf{shift}}_{i} for some ii. Such an element ϵ\epsilon is minimal if it does not appear on any other line of the stack, since if it doesn’t then it can’t be greater than any other element appearing in the stack. Conversely, if ϵ\epsilon does appear on another line of the stack then on that line it cannot appear in the first place (since those letters differ by d=K−md=K-m from one line to the next), and consequently ϵ\epsilon is greater in 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) than the letters preceding it on that line. Similarly, the only elements that can be maximal in the poset 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) are those appearing as the last letter of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i{\mathsf{shift}}_{i} for some ii and such an element is maximal if and only if it appears on no other line of the stack. Suppose 1 belongs to 𝐩\mathbf{p}. Then the maximum possible value of the first element of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0} is mm, so the maximum possible value of the first letter of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍1{\mathsf{shift}}_{1} is m+(K−m)=Km+(K-m)=K, which is also found in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0}, so the first letter of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍1{\mathsf{shift}}_{1} cannot be minimal in 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j). Analogous reasoning shows that the first letter of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i{\mathsf{shift}}_{i} for any i>1i>1 cannot be minimal in 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j). The first letter ℓ\ell of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0} is minimal, however, when 1 belongs to 𝐩\mathbf{p}, as we now show: If m≤K/2m\leq K/2 then ℓ\ell is at most K/2K/2 and the least element of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍1{\mathsf{shift}}_{1} is 1+K−m>K/21+K-m>K/2, so ℓ\ell does not appear in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍1{\mathsf{shift}}_{1} (or on any later line of the stack). If m>K/2m>K/2 then 1 cannot appear in the intersection of 𝐩\mathbf{p} and 𝐬\mathbf{s} since if it did then it of course would be the smallest element of each. But then the smallest element of the prefix would have fewer greater letters after it than the smallest letter of the suffix, so they couldn’t be isomorphic. So if 1 belongs to 𝐩\mathbf{p} then the maximum possible value of ℓ\ell is K−mK-m and the least element in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍1{\mathsf{shift}}_{1} is 1+K−m1+K-m, so again ℓ\ell does not appear in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍1{\mathsf{shift}}_{1}. The argument in the case when 1 belongs to the suffix is similar, and analogous arguments prove the claims about the position of KK. Finally, if 1 belongs to neither 𝐩\mathbf{p} nor 𝐬\mathbf{s} then an analysis similar to the one above shows that the first letter of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i{\mathsf{shift}}_{i} for any ii cannot appear on any other line of the stack, and an analogous argument applies when KK belongs neither to 𝐩\mathbf{p} nor 𝐬\mathbf{s}. The last part of the theorem follows from its preceding parts. ∎

Before deriving a corollary of Proposition 5.12 we make the following definition. Note first that every pattern-packing poset 𝒫\mathcal{P} is connected, by virtue of the occurrences of the pattern overlapping.

Definition 5.13.

A pattern poset 𝒫\mathcal{P} whose Hasse diagram, viewed as an undirected graph, is a tree is referred to as a tree poset or just a tree. If, in addition, 𝒫\mathcal{P} has a unique minimal and a unique maximal element then 𝒫\mathcal{P} is a chain.

A poset 𝒫\mathcal{P} being a chain means that there is a total order on the elements of 𝒫\mathcal{P}.

If m≥K/2m\geq K/2 then each of 1 and KK belongs to either prefix or suffix, and so 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) has a unique minimal and a unique maximal element by Proposition 5.12:

Corollary 5.14.

For overlap m≥K/2m\geq K/2, if 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) is a tree then it is a chain.

In the following definition we restrict the pattern π\pi to not have 1 in its suffix, since that simplifies the definition and the proof of the following theorem. This causes no loss of generality, since if 1 is in the suffix we obtain an equivalent pattern by reversing π\pi.

Definition 5.15.

Let π\pi be a KK-pattern that doesn’t have 1 in its mm-suffix. Let MpM_{p} be the greatest element of the mm-prefix of π\pi and let MsM_{s} be the greatest element of the mm-suffix of π\pi.

The bottom element of 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) is the first letter of the first line of the stack for 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j).

The top element of 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) is the last letter of the first line of the stack for 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) if Mp>MsM_{p}>M_{s}, but otherwise it is the last letter of the last line of the stack.

The core of 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) is the interval between the top and bottom elements of 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j).

A branch of 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) is a nonempty connected subset of 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j), disjoint from the core and maximal with respect to inclusion. □\square

See Figure 5.2 for an example of the core and branches of a poset.

For a KK-pattern π\pi and overlap mm recall that the interfix of π\pi is πm+1​πm+2​…​πK−m\pi_{m+1}\pi_{m+2}\ldots\pi_{K-m}, that is, the segment of letters between the mm-prefix and mm-suffix of π\pi. For m>K/2m>K/2, the interfix is understood to be empty. The length of a chain is its number of elements.

As in the preceding definition, in the following theorem we restrict the pattern π\pi to not have 1 in its suffix but also, when m≤K/2m\leq K/2, to have the least element of its mm-prefix be smaller than the least element of its mm-suffix, and to have increasing prefix and suffix, since this simplifies the proof, without losing generality, by the lemmas of Section 3.

Theorem 5.16.

Let π\pi be a KK-pattern with mm-prefix 𝐩\mathbf{p} and mm-suffix 𝐬\mathbf{s} that does not have 1 in 𝐬\mathbf{s}, where the least element of 𝐩\mathbf{p} is smaller than the least element of 𝐬\mathbf{s}, and, when m≤K/2m\leq K/2, assume 𝐩\mathbf{p} and 𝐬\mathbf{s} are increasing.

Let MpM_{p} be the greatest element of 𝐩\mathbf{p} and let MsM_{s} be the greatest element of 𝐬\mathbf{s}.
Let 1,2,3,…,a1,2,3,\ldots,a be the maximal sequence of successive values, starting with 1, contained (in any order) in the interfix of π\pi and set a=0a=0 if the sequence is empty.
Let K−b+1,K−b+2,…,KK-b+1,K-b+2,\ldots,K be the maximal sequence of successive values, ending with KK, contained (in any order) in the interfix of π\pi and set b=0b=0 if the sequence is empty.

If either sequence above is empty the corresponding following statements are omitted.

Then:

  1. 1.

    For each i>0i>0, the first aa elements of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i{\mathsf{shift}}_{i} form a branch in 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j).

  2. 2.

    If Mp>MsM_{p}>M_{s} then, for each i>0i>0,the last bb elements of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i{\mathsf{shift}}_{i} form a branch in 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j).

  3. 3.

    If Mp<MsM_{p}<M_{s} then, for each i<j−1i<j-1, the last bb elements of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i{\mathsf{shift}}_{i} form a branch in 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j).

  4. 4.

    Each branch of 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) is a chain, connected by a single edge to the core of 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j).

  5. 5.

    All other elements of the stack belong to the core.

  6. 6.

    Every chain of maximal length in 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) contains the top and bottom elements of 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j).

Proof.

The case j=1j=1 is trivial, since 𝒫πm​(1){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(1) is a single chain. Suppose first that m>K/2m>K/2. Then neither 11 nor KK can belong to the intersection of 𝐩\mathbf{p} and 𝐬\mathbf{s}, for if 1 belonged to both then it would be the least element of both, but in different positions, so they couldn’t be order isomorphic. The case for KK is analogous. Thus 11 belongs only to 𝐩\mathbf{p}, since it is assumed to not belong to 𝐬\mathbf{s}, and KK belongs either to 𝐩\mathbf{p} or 𝐬\mathbf{s}.

By Proposition 5.12, the poset has a unique minimal and a unique maximal element. This minimum must be the first letter of the first line, because the first letter of every later line also belongs to the preceding line. Namely, since 1 is in 𝐩\mathbf{p}, and not in the intersection of 𝐩\mathbf{p} and 𝐬\mathbf{s}, its place in π\pi is at most K−m<mK-m<m, so the first element f0f_{0} of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0} is therefore strictly smaller than mm, and the first element fif_{i} of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i{\mathsf{shift}}_{i}, for any i>0i>0, is strictly smaller than m+i⁡(K−m)=K+(i−1)​(K−m)m+i(K-m)=K+(i-1)(K-m), which is the greatest letter in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i−1{\mathsf{shift}}_{i-1}, so fif_{i} belongs to 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i−1{\mathsf{shift}}_{i-1}.

Analogous arguments show that if KK belongs to 𝐩\mathbf{p}, each later line’s last letter belongs to the preceding line and if KK belongs to 𝐬\mathbf{s}, each line’s last letter, except for the last line, belongs to the following line. The minimum and maximum are therefore the stated bottom and top. Since each is comparable to every element of the stack, every maximal chain contains both, the core is the entire poset and there are no branches, as a=b=0a=b=0.

Now suppose m≤K/2m\leq K/2, that 𝐩\mathbf{p} and 𝐬\mathbf{s} are increasing, that the minimum of 𝐩\mathbf{p} is smaller than the minimum of 𝐬\mathbf{s} (and thus that 1 is not in 𝐬\mathbf{s}). If a>0a>0 then, since the elements 1,2,…,a1,2,\ldots,a belong to the interfix, and thus are in places greater than mm, the first aa elements of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i{\mathsf{shift}}_{i} for i>0i>0 are greater than m+i⁡(K−m)=K+(i−1)​(K−m)m+i(K-m)=K+(i-1)(K-m), the greatest element of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i−1{\mathsf{shift}}_{i-1}, and therefore do not belong to 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍k{\mathsf{shift}}_{k} for any k<ik<i. Their labels are at most (K−m)+i⁡(K−m)=(i+1)​(K−m)(K-m)+i(K-m)=(i+1)(K-m), since they precede the mm-suffix, so they do not belong to any later line either. Thus each occurs on just one line, so they form a chain whose only attachment to the rest of the poset is via the edge to the element in place a+1a+1.

When b>0b>0, a similar argument shows that the last bb elements of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i{\mathsf{shift}}_{i} for i<j−1i<j-1 do not belong to 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍k{\mathsf{shift}}_{k} for any k>ik>i, nor do the last bb elements of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i{\mathsf{shift}}_{i} for i>0i>0 belong to 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍k{\mathsf{shift}}_{k} for any k<ik<i, so regardless of whether the top element is in the first or last line of the stack, the last bb elements on each line specified in the statement cannot, in 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j), be below the top element.

We now show that the bottom element, the first element of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0}, is, in 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j), below the element in place a+1a+1, and thus below all elements in places after the aa-th, in each 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i{\mathsf{shift}}_{i} for i>0i>0, which excludes only the aa branch elements at the beginning of each of these lines. The letter in place a+1a+1 in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0} is 1, because 1 is in the place determined by the first letter of 𝐩\mathbf{p} (which is assumed increasing), and this letter must be a+1a+1, since that’s the smallest letter not in the interfix, and that letter cannot be in 𝐬\mathbf{s}, whose least letter is greater than that of 𝐩\mathbf{p}.
