Thus, the letter in place a+1a+1 in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i{\mathsf{shift}}_{i} is 1+i⁡(K−m)1+i(K-m), which occurs in place 𝐬1\mathbf{s}_{1} of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i−1{\mathsf{shift}}_{i-1}. Since 𝐬1>𝐩1=a+1\mathbf{s}_{1}>\mathbf{p}_{1}=a+1, induction from the first line proves the claim.

Again, similar arguments show that the top element is greater than or equal to all elements in places up to K−bK-b in each 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i{\mathsf{shift}}_{i}.

Consequently, the elements other than those described as branches in the statement are exactly the core. Since each of the sets of elements described as branches has been shown to form a chain, connected by a single edge to the core, it does indeed constitute a branch.

It remains to consider longest chains, which are necessarily maximal. A maximal chain 𝒞\mathcal{C} not starting at the bottom element starts in a branch, consisting of the first aa elements of some 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i{\mathsf{shift}}_{i} for i>0i>0, and must contain all of those aa elements, since the last one of these is the only one that is connected to the core of the poset, at a vertex vv, which is the letter in place a+1a+1 in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i{\mathsf{shift}}_{i}. But that letter, as shown above, also belongs to 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i−1{\mathsf{shift}}_{i-1} and there lies to the right of place a+1a+1. Thus, replacing the initial aa elements of the chain 𝒞\mathcal{C} by all the letters in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i−1{\mathsf{shift}}_{i-1} up to and including the one in place a+1a+1, while retaining vv and the rest of 𝒞\mathcal{C}, we have lengthened the chain 𝒞\mathcal{C} by at least one element. So a chain not starting at the bottom element cannot have maximal length. Analogous arguments show the top element must belong to any chain of maximal length. ∎

The following are consequences of the proof of Theorem 5.16.

Porism 5.17.

Let aa and bb be as defined in the statement of Theorem 5.16.

  • ∙\bullet

    Branches determined by the sequence 1,2,…,a1,2,\ldots,a go downwards from the core, that is, their elements are below the vertex connecting them to the core, and they all have the same length aa.

  • ∙\bullet

    Branches determined by the sequence K−b+1,K−b+2,…,KK-b+1,K-b+2,\ldots,K go upwards from the core, that is, their elements are above the vertex connecting them to the core, and they all have the same length bb.

  • ∙\bullet

    If the prefix and suffix of π\pi between them contain both 11 and KK, in particular if m≥K/2m\geq K/2, then 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) has no branches.

An upper bound of two elements a,ba,b in a poset 𝒫\mathcal{P} is an element xx such that a,b≤xa,b\leq x. A least upper bound of aa and bb is an upper bound xx such that x≤yx\leq y for any upper bound yy of aa and bb. A greatest lower bound is defined analogously, with ’≤\leq’ replaced by ’≥\geq’. An order theoretic lattice is a poset where each pair of elements has a least upper bound and a greatest lower bound.

Theorem 5.18.

The core of a pattern poset 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) is a lattice. In particular, if the mm-suffix and mm-prefix of π\pi between them contain both 1 and KK then 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) is a lattice. Also, the poset obtained from 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) by adding an element greater than all elements of 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) and an element smaller than all elements of 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) is a lattice.

Proof.

Since the core has a bottom and a top, every pair of its elements has an upper and a lower bound. We show, more generally, that whenever two elements of 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) have common upper bounds, they have a least upper bound.

Suppose a,ba,b have common upper bounds but no least upper bound. They must therefore have two distinct common upper bounds xx and yy that are minimal with respect to being common upper bounds, and they are necessarily incomparable. Choose four saturated chains, from aa to xx, aa to yy, bb to xx and bb to yy.

Every element other than x,yx,y on either chain from aa is incomparable to every element other than x,yx,y on either chain from bb. Namely, if uu is on a chain from aa and vv on a chain from bb, with u≤vu\leq v, then vv is a common upper bound for a,ba,b strictly below xx or yy, contradicting minimality. The case v≤uv\leq u is analogous.

Consecutive elements of each chain appear together on some line of the stack, since their comparison is a cover relation, as the chains are saturated. By Lemma 5.7, the lines containing elements of either chain from aa, with x,yx,y omitted, form an interval of lines, for each chain meets consecutive lines, and the two chains meet at aa. The same holds for the chains from bb. These two intervals are disjoint, by the incomparability established above. Assume, without loss of generality, that the interval for the chains from aa precedes that for the chains from bb.

Let 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍r{\mathsf{shift}}_{r} be the last line of the former interval. Each of x,yx,y occurs on a line in each interval, since it occurs together with its predecessor on each of the two chains ending there. By Lemma 5.7, both xx and yy therefore occur on 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍r{\mathsf{shift}}_{r}. This makes them comparable, a contradiction. Hence a,ba,b have a least upper bound. Since the dual of a pattern poset is a pattern poset this also applies to greatest lower bounds.

If the prefix and suffix between them contain both 11 and KK then the core is the whole poset, so 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) is a lattice.

After adjoining 1^\widehat{1} and 0^\widehat{0}, existing least upper and greatest lower bounds remain unchanged. A pair with no common upper bound now has least upper bound 1^\widehat{1}, and a pair with no common lower bound has greatest lower bound 0^\widehat{0}, since these are common bounds, and the only possible such. The resulting poset is therefore a lattice. ∎

Note that Theorem 5.18 in particular implies that in a pattern poset two distinct elements cannot both cover (or be covered by) another two distinct elements, since that would violate unique least upper (and greatest lower) bounds.

5.2 Chains and tree posets

We now give necessary and sufficient conditions for a pattern packing poset to be a tree, or a chain. Figures 5.3 and 5.4 supply examples. (Of course, the poset for one occurrence of a pattern is always a chain.)

The following theorem characterizes the trees among pattern posets. The idea of the proof is that having a cycle in the Hasse diagram, seen as a graph, implies that some four elements, a<x,y<ba<x,y<b, of that cycle must satisfy the conditions in the theorem, and conversely. We first need a lemma.

A simple cycle in a graph is a sequence of vertices, each connected by edges to its predecessor and successor, and such that the only repeated vertex in the sequence is the first and last one. If a graph has a cycle then it necessarily has a simple cycle. A chain CC is saturated if no element of the poset lies strictly between two consecutive elements of CC. A chain x1<x2<⋯<xnx_{1}<x_{2}<\cdots<x_{n} being saturated is equivalent to each of its inequalities being a cover relation. Note that if a<ba<b is a cover relation in a pattern poset then aa must immediately precede bb on some line of the stack. The converse is not true in general, because we might have another element xx between aa and bb on some other line of the stack.

In the remainder of the paper, the interior of a vector or sequence of any sort is that thing itself take away its first and last element.

Lemma 5.19.

If a pattern poset 𝒫\mathcal{P} is not a tree then it has a simple cycle that consists of the two elements aa and bb and two saturated chains CC and DD that are disjoint apart from both having aa as minimum and bb as maximum, and such that each element in the interior of CC is incomparable to every element in the interior of DD.

Proof.

If a pattern poset is not a tree then it has a simple cycle, seen as a graph, and such a cycle must belong entirely to the core of 𝒫\mathcal{P}. Namely, a cycle that wanders onto a branch can only be closed by leaving that branch again, via its only edge connected to the core, and so would not be simple.

Let aa be the smallest element of the core of 𝒫\mathcal{P} that is covered by two different elements x1x_{1} and y1y_{1}. (If aa is not the bottom element of 𝒫\mathcal{P} then it is the maximum element in the chain of elements at the bottom of 𝒫\mathcal{P} all of whose other elements are covered by only one element.) Since the core of 𝒫\mathcal{P} is a lattice, by Theorem 5.18, x1x_{1} and y1y_{1} have a least upper bound bb. Then 𝒫\mathcal{P} has two saturated chains

C:a<x1<x2<⋯<xr<b​and​D:a<y1<y2<⋯<ys<b,C:a<x_{1}<x_{2}<\cdots<x_{r}<b~~~\mathrm{and}~~~D:a<y_{1}<y_{2}<\cdots<y_{s}<b,

that are disjoint apart from aa and bb, since if xi=yℓx_{i}=y_{\ell} for some ii and ℓ\ell then xix_{i} would be an upper bound for x1x_{1} and y1y_{1}, so bb would not be a least upper bound for x1x_{1} and y1y_{1}. Moreover, if xi<yℓx_{i}<y_{\ell} for some ii and ℓ\ell then yℓy_{\ell} would be an upper bound for x1x_{1} and y1y_{1}, so bb would not be a least upper bound, and analogously if yℓ<xiy_{\ell}<x_{i}. ∎

We now present a theorem that completely characterizes pattern posets that are trees, in terms of the stack. Note that if the overlap mm is at most half the length KK of the pattern here then, by Lemma 5.8, any elements a,ba,b that appear on two lines of the stack appear only on two adjacent lines, which makes the proof almost trivial.

Theorem 5.20.

A pattern poset 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) has a cycle if and only if there are two lines 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍s,𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍t{\mathsf{shift}}_{s},{\mathsf{shift}}_{t}, with s<ts<t, and elements a,b,x,ya,b,x,y satisfying the following conditions:

  • ∙\bullet

    No line contains both xx and yy.

  • ∙\bullet

    On 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍s{\mathsf{shift}}_{s}, xx lies between aa and bb.

  • ∙\bullet

    On 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍t{\mathsf{shift}}_{t}, yy lies between aa and bb.

  • ∙\bullet

    No element lies between aa and bb on two distinct lines among 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍s,𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍s+1,…,𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍t{\mathsf{shift}}_{s},{\mathsf{shift}}_{s+1},\ldots,{\mathsf{shift}}_{t}.

Proof.

Suppose first that there are elements and lines as described. We show that xx and yy are incomparable.

Any comparison between xx and yy can be established using only the lines from 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍s{\mathsf{shift}}_{s} to 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍t{\mathsf{shift}}_{t}. Indeed, any part of a comparison passing through earlier lines has its entry and exit letters on 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍s{\mathsf{shift}}_{s}, and can therefore be replaced by their comparison on that line. The same argument applies to lines after 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍t{\mathsf{shift}}_{t}.

If xx and yy were comparable, a sequence of comparisons on these lines would consequently establish x<yx<y, or y<xy<x. Since no line contains both, this sequence must pass from one line to another at some intermediate element zz. But zz then lies strictly between aa and bb on both lines, contrary to the last condition. Thus xx and yy are incomparable. Since both lie between aa and bb, there are two distinct saturated chains from aa to bb, whose union contains a cycle. Hence 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) is not a tree.

Conversely, suppose 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) is not a tree. By Lemma 5.19, it has an interval that is not a chain. Choose such an interval [a,b][a,b] with as few elements as possible. Every proper subinterval is then a chain.

Distinct maximal chains in [a,b][a,b] can meet only at aa and bb, and their interior elements are pairwise incomparable. Otherwise, a meeting or comparison between them would give two distinct maximal chains in a proper subinterval. Since aa is covered by at most two elements, [a,b][a,b] therefore consists of exactly two saturated chains CC and DD, disjoint apart from their endpoints.

The lines containing interior elements of CC are consecutive: each element occurs on consecutive lines, and consecutive elements of CC occur together on some line because their comparison is a cover relation. The same holds for DD. These two sets of lines are disjoint, since no line can contain incomparable elements. We may assume that the lines containing interior elements of CC precede those containing interior elements of DD.

Let 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍s{\mathsf{shift}}_{s} be the last line containing an interior element xx of CC, and let 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍t{\mathsf{shift}}_{t} be the first line containing an interior element yy of DD. Each of aa and bb occurs on a line with an interior element of each chain, by the cover relations at the ends of the chains. Consequently, both aa and bb occur on every line from 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍s{\mathsf{shift}}_{s} to 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍t{\mathsf{shift}}_{t}. Thus xx and yy lie between aa and bb on their respective lines, and no line contains both.

Finally, every element strictly between aa and bb belongs to CC or DD. Among the lines from 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍s{\mathsf{shift}}_{s} to 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍t{\mathsf{shift}}_{t}, an interior element of CC can occur only on 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍s{\mathsf{shift}}_{s}, and an interior element of DD only on 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍t{\mathsf{shift}}_{t}. No such element can therefore occur on two of these lines. This proves the last condition and completes the proof. ∎

An example illustrating why in the above theorem it is not enough to examine just the two lines 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍s{\mathsf{shift}}_{s} and 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍t{\mathsf{shift}}_{t} is π=13526748\pi=13526748 with overlap 5, whose 3-stack is

𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0=14273568𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍1=4751068911𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍2=7108139111214\begin{array}[]{ccccccccccccc}{\mathsf{shift}}_{0}=&1&4&2&7&3&5&6&8\\ {\mathsf{shift}}_{1}=&4&7&5&10&6&8&9&11\\ {\mathsf{shift}}_{2}=&7&10&8&13&9&11&12&14\end{array}

With a=7,b=8,x=3,y=10a=7,b=8,x=3,y=10 we see that (i) no line contains both 3 and 10, (ii) in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0} 3 lies between 7 and 8, (iii) in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍2{\mathsf{shift}}_{2} 10 lies between 7 and 8, and (iv) on these two lines there is no shared element between 7 and 8. But, 5 lies between 7 and 8 in both 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0} and 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍1{\mathsf{shift}}_{1}, so 3≺5≺103\prec 5\prec 10 in 𝒫π5​(3){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{5}(3) and this poset has no cycle, it is in fact a chain.

In [5, Section 2.2], Dwyer and Elizalde describe the posets we are discussing here in the case of overlap 1, for patterns they call non-overlapping, which are those whose occurrences can overlap in at most one position.

Corollary 5.21.

For overlap 1 and any KK-pattern π\pi, the poset 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) is a tree. It is a chain (for any j>1j>1) if and only if the prefix of π\pi is 1 and the suffix is KK or vice versa.

Proof.

For overlap 1 and i≠ℓi\neq\ell, 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i{\mathsf{shift}}_{i} and 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍ℓ{\mathsf{shift}}_{\ell} can have at most one element in common. So, there are no pairs of repeated elements a,ba,b to form a cycle. By Proposition 5.12, 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) has a unique minimal element and a unique maximal element if and only if the prefix and suffix contain both 1 and KK, and a tree is a chain if and only if it has a unique minimal and a unique maximal element. ∎

Recall from Corollary 5.14 that if 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) is a tree and m≥K/2m\geq K/2 then 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) is necessarily a chain. We now give necessary and sufficient conditions for this when m<K/2m<K/2. This characterization also holds for m>K/2m>K/2, but assuming m≤K/2m\leq K/2 simplifies the proof.

Proposition 5.22.

Let π\pi be a KK-pattern. If m≤K/2m\leq K/2 and 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) is a tree then 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) is a chain if and only if it satisfies the following conditions:

  • ∙\bullet

    If an element xx of 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) is the leftmost repeated element on two different lines of the stack then at least one of the two sets of elements to the left of xx is empty.

  • ∙\bullet

    If an element xx of 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) is the rightmost repeated element on two different lines of the stack then at least one of the two sets of elements to the right of xx is empty.

Proof.

The case j=1j=1 is immediate. Let j>1j>1. A tree poset is a chain if and only if it has a unique minimal element and a unique maximal element.

If 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) has a unique minimal element and a unique maximal element then, by Proposition 5.12, the mm-prefix and mm-suffix of π\pi between them contain both 1 and KK. If 1 is contained in the mm-prefix then the first element of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0} is at most mm, and consequently the first element

of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i{\mathsf{shift}}_{i} is at most m+i⁡(K−m)m+i(K-m). But the largest element of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i−1{\mathsf{shift}}_{i-1}, for i>0i>0, is K+(i−1)​(K−m)=m+i⁡(K−m)K+(i-1)(K-m)=m+i(K-m), so the first element of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i{\mathsf{shift}}_{i} also appears in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i−1{\mathsf{shift}}_{i-1}, and must consequently be the leftmost repeated element in both, by Lemma 5.6. Also, since m≤K/2m\leq K/2, no element appears on more than two lines of the stack, by Lemma 5.8. Thus the set of elements to its left on one of the two lines is empty. The cases when 1 belongs to the suffix, and when KK belongs to the prefix or suffix, are analogous.

Conversely, suppose 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) does not have a unique minimal element. Then, by Proposition 5.12, 1 belongs neither to the mm-prefix nor the mm-suffix of π\pi. Since 1 does not belong to the mm-prefix, the first element of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0} is at least m+1m+1 and, in general, the first element of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i{\mathsf{shift}}_{i} is at least m+1+i⁡(K−m)m+1+i(K-m), which is greater than the greatest element of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i−1{\mathsf{shift}}_{i-1}, which is K+(i−1)​(K−m)K+(i-1)(K-m). Thus, the leftmost element in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i{\mathsf{shift}}_{i} is not repeated in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i−1{\mathsf{shift}}_{i-1}. Also, since 1 does not belong to the mm-suffix, the first element of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0} is at most K−mK-m and, in general, the first element of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i−1{\mathsf{shift}}_{i-1} is at most K−m+(i−1)​(K−m)=i⁡(K−m)K-m+(i-1)(K-m)=i(K-m), which is smaller than the smallest element of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i{\mathsf{shift}}_{i}, which is 1+i⁡(K−m)1+i(K-m). Thus, the leftmost element in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i−1{\mathsf{shift}}_{i-1} is not repeated in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i{\mathsf{shift}}_{i}.

Therefore, the leftmost element ℓ\ell that appears in both 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i{\mathsf{shift}}_{i} and 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍i−1{\mathsf{shift}}_{i-1} is not in the first place in either, and thus ℓ\ell has an element to its left on both lines, and two such elements can not be identical since that would constitute a different leftmost repeated element. Both sets of elements preceding it are therefore nonempty, contrary to the first condition. The case when 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) does not have a unique maximal element is analogous. ∎

We now wish to express the above results, when m≤K/2m\leq K/2, in terms of a KK-pattern π\pi rather than its stack. To simplify the argument we assume, without loss of generality (see Remark 5.9), that the elements of the prefix and suffix, respectively, of π\pi are in increasing order. We then define the gap vector of the mm-prefix 𝐩=𝐩1​𝐩2​…​𝐩m\mathbf{p}=\mathbf{p}_{1}\mathbf{p}_{2}\ldots\mathbf{p}_{m} as

𝐝𝐩=(𝐝𝐩1,𝐝𝐩2,…,𝐝𝐩m+1)=(𝐩1−1,𝐩2−𝐩1−1,…,𝐩m−𝐩m−1−1,K−𝐩m).\mathbf{dp}=(\mathbf{dp}_{1},\mathbf{dp}_{2},\ldots,\mathbf{dp}_{m+1})=(\mathbf{p}_{1}-1,\mathbf{p}_{2}-\mathbf{p}_{1}-1,\ldots,\mathbf{p}_{m}-\mathbf{p}_{m-1}-1,K-\mathbf{p}_{m}).

The gap vector 𝐝𝐬\mathbf{ds} for the suffix 𝐬=𝐬1​𝐬2​…​𝐬m\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}_{1}\mathbf{s}_{2}\ldots\mathbf{s}_{m} is defined in the analogous way, with 𝐬i\mathbf{s}_{i} replacing 𝐩i\mathbf{p}_{i}. Note that 𝐝𝐩\mathbf{dp} and 𝐝𝐬\mathbf{ds} both have length m+1m+1.

Theorem 5.23.

Let π\pi be a KK-pattern, m≤K/2m\leq K/2 and j≥2j\geq 2. The poset 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) is a tree if and only if the interiors of the gap vectors of the mm-prefix and mm-suffix of π\pi are empty or have dot product 0. Also, 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) is a chain if and only if the dot product of the gap vectors is 0.

Proof.

Note that in the definition of the gap vectors 𝐝𝐩\mathbf{dp} and 𝐝𝐬\mathbf{ds}, the mm-prefix and the mm-suffix are assumed to be increasing.

The ℓ\ell-th coordinate 𝐝𝐩ℓ\mathbf{dp}_{\ell} of the gap vector of the mm-prefix 𝐩\mathbf{p} of π\pi, when 1<ℓ≤m1<\ell\leq m, counts the elements of π\pi that are strictly between 𝐩ℓ−1\mathbf{p}_{\ell-1} and 𝐩ℓ\mathbf{p}_{\ell} in size, and likewise for the mm-suffix 𝐬\mathbf{s}. The mm elements that appear both in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍r{\mathsf{shift}}_{r} and 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍r+1{\mathsf{shift}}_{r+1} in the stack for 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) appear in places s1,s2,…,sms_{1},s_{2},\ldots,s_{m} in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍r{\mathsf{shift}}_{r} and in places p1,p2,…,pmp_{1},p_{2},\ldots,p_{m} in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍r+1{\mathsf{shift}}_{r+1}. Thus, between the element aa in place sis_{i} and the element bb in place si+1s_{i+1} in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍r{\mathsf{shift}}_{r}, we have 𝐝𝐬i+1\mathbf{ds}_{i+1} elements, and between the element in place pip_{i}, which is necessarily aa, and the element in place pi+1p_{i+1}, necessarily bb, in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍r+1{\mathsf{shift}}_{r+1}, we have 𝐝𝐩i+1\mathbf{dp}_{i+1} elements. Also, between aa and bb on these two lines of the stack there are no repeated elements.

Thus, the elements aa and bb that appear in both 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍r{\mathsf{shift}}_{r} and 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍r+1{\mathsf{shift}}_{r+1} (which have no repeated element between them) have some elements between them on both lines if and only if 𝐝𝐩i+1⋅𝐝𝐬i+1≠0\mathbf{dp}_{i+1}\cdot\mathbf{ds}_{i+1}\neq 0. This applies to all coordinates of the interiors of 𝐝𝐩\mathbf{dp} and 𝐝𝐬\mathbf{ds}, and therefore, by Theorem 5.20, 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) is a tree if and only if the interiors of 𝐝𝐩\mathbf{dp} and 𝐝𝐬\mathbf{ds} have dot product 0 or are empty, as a repeated element can only appear on two successive lines of the stack when m≤K/2m\leq K/2, by Lemma 5.8.

For 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) to be a chain it must, in addition to the dot product of the interiors of 𝐝𝐩\mathbf{dp} and 𝐝𝐬\mathbf{ds} being 0, have a unique minimal element and a unique maximal element. By Proposition 5.12, that is equivalent to 𝐩\mathbf{p} and 𝐬\mathbf{s} containing, between them, both 1 and KK. That, in turn, is equivalent to (𝐝𝐩1=0​ or ​𝐝𝐬1=0)(\mathbf{dp}_{1}=0\text{ or }\mathbf{ds}_{1}=0) and (𝐝𝐩m+1=0​ or ​𝐝𝐬m+1=0)(\mathbf{dp}_{m+1}=0\text{ or }\mathbf{ds}_{m+1}=0), which is equivalent to 𝐝𝐩1⋅𝐝𝐬1=𝐝𝐩m+1⋅𝐝𝐬m+1=0\mathbf{dp}_{1}\cdot\mathbf{ds}_{1}=\mathbf{dp}_{m+1}\cdot\mathbf{ds}_{m+1}=0, in which case the dot product of the entire gap vectors 𝐝𝐩\mathbf{dp} and 𝐝𝐬\mathbf{ds} is 0. ∎

As an example, if π=124635\pi=124635 and m=2m=2 (see Figure 5.5) then 𝐝𝐩=(0,0,4)\mathbf{dp}=(0,0,4) and 𝐝𝐬=(2,1,1)\mathbf{ds}=(2,1,1). The vector 𝐝𝐩\mathbf{dp} thus gives the number of elements in π\pi that lie strictly between successive entries of 𝐩\mathbf{p} in size, except that its first entry is the number of elements in π\pi strictly smaller than the first (and smallest) element of 𝐩\mathbf{p} and the last entry is the number of elements strictly greater than the last (and largest) element of 𝐩\mathbf{p}, and likewise for 𝐝𝐬\mathbf{ds}. Looking at the first two lines of the stack for π=124635\pi=124635 in Figure 5.5, we see that 𝐝𝐬=(2,1,1)\mathbf{ds}=(2,1,1) corresponds to the fact that on the first line of the stack there are two elements before the first repeated element 5, one element between 5 and the other repeated element, the 6, and one element after 6 on the first line. Similarly, 𝐝𝐩=(0,0,4)\mathbf{dp}=(0,0,4) corresponds to the fact that on the second line there is no element preceding 5, no element between the 5 and the 6 and four elements after the 6. The dot product of the interiors is 1⋅0=01\cdot 0=0, and the poset in question is a tree. It is not a chain, since the last coordinates of both gap vectors are positive. If we were to switch 5 and 6 in π\pi, however, the resulting poset would become a chain, and 𝐝𝐬=(2,2,0)\mathbf{ds}=(2,2,0).

If 11 belongs to the prefix (or KK to the suffix) of a KK-pattern whose poset is a tree then the enumeration of linear extensions has a product formula:

Proposition 5.24.

Let π\pi be a KK-pattern with 1 in its prefix, whose poset is a tree. Let v1<⋯<vtv_{1}<\cdots<v_{t} be the vertices of the core that branches are attached to, let ℓ\ell be the length of the branches, and let NiN_{i} be the number of vertices strictly above viv_{i} and not on the branch attached to viv_{i}. Then

|𝒮πm​(j)|=∏i=1t(Ni+ℓℓ).|\mathcal{S}_{\pi}^{m}(j)|=\prod_{i=1}^{t}\binom{N_{i}+\ell}{\ell}.
Proof.

It follows from Porism 5.17, since 1 is in the prefix, that all branches go upwards from the core, which in a tree is necessarily a chain. Now, everything outside the lowest branch is either weakly below its attachment to the core or above that vertex, so its elements must in a linear extension come after the former, but can be placed arbitrarily with respect to the latter. This gives the first factor, and induction gives the formula. ∎

For a consecutive prefix the numbers NiN_{i} have a particularly simple form, giving the following product. Recall that if m≥K/2m\geq K/2 then a corresponding tree poset is a chain, so nothing is lost by the restriction m≤K/2m\leq K/2 here:

Proposition 5.25.

Let π\pi be a pattern with prefix 12⋯m12\cdots m and increasing suffix ending in ss, where m≤K/2m\leq K/2. Let d=K−md=K-m and ℓ=K−s\ell=K-s. Then

|𝒮πm​(j)|=∏i=0j−1(i​d+ℓℓ).|\mathcal{S}_{\pi}^{m}(j)|=\prod_{i=0}^{j-1}\binom{id+\ell}{\ell}.
Proof.

Since 1 is in the mm-prefix of π\pi, all branches of 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) go upwards, and each has length ℓ\ell, by Porism 5.17. Because the branches rise at regular intervals from the core (which in a tree is a chain), to count linear extensions we may assume that the jj-th occurrence adds a branch below the previous branches rather than above them. The elements of that branch are incomparable to all (j−1)​d(j-1)d elements above the node NN of the core that the branch is attached to, and in a linear extension the ℓ\ell elements of the branch can be placed anywhere with respect to those elements, but must lie above all elements below and including NN. This gives the factor ((j−1)​d+ℓℓ)\binom{(j-1)d+\ell}{\ell} and a straightforward inductive argument completes the proof. ∎

The special case of Proposition 5.25 when m=1m=1 is Proposition 26 in [3], see also Figure 12 in [8].

In particular, the proposition applies to every overlap-11 pattern whose first letter is 11.

Definition 5.26.

For integers n≥1n\geq 1 and k≥1k\geq 1, the kk-shift factorial of nn is n!k:=∏0≤i<n/k(n−ik)\displaystyle n!_{k}:=\prod_{0\leq i<n/k}(n-ik).

Thus, n!kn!_{k} is the product of all positive integers in the sequence n,(n−k),(n−2​k),⋯n,(n-k),(n-2k),\cdots.

For overlap 1 we get the following special case:

Corollary 5.27.

Let π\pi be a KK-pattern with π1=1\pi_{1}=1 and πK=K−1\pi_{K}=K-1. The number of permutations that (1,j)(1,j)-pack π\pi is n!K−1n!_{K-1}, where n=K+(j−2)​(K−1)n=K+(j-2)(K-1).

An example of Proposition 5.25 is the pattern 125634 with overlap 2, where d=4d=4, ℓ=2\ell=2, whose poset is shown in Figure 5.6. The same figure shows the poset for the pattern 163425 with overlap 2. An argument similar to the one in Proposition 5.25, also analyzing the effect on the poset of adding a new occurrence, shows that all KK-patterns π\pi with mm-prefix 123​…​(m−1)​K123\ldots(m-1)K and any increasing mm-suffix have enumeration of the same form as in Proposition 5.25. Namely, a straightforward analysis of the stack of the poset for such a pattern shows that each new occurrence adds K−mK-m elements to the right edge of the Hasse diagram, when drawn as in Figure 5.6.

As with the argument for the tree, we can instead add a new first occurrence. Its ℓ\ell letters between K−1K-1 and KK form a chain incomparable to the (j−1)​d(j-1)d old elements strictly between these vertices. All remaining new letters are comparable to every element. Thus the new factor is ((j−1)​d+ℓℓ)\binom{(j-1)d+\ell}{\ell}.

Proposition 5.28.

Let m≥2m\geq 2 and let π\pi be a KK-pattern with mm-prefix 123​…​(m−1)​K123\ldots(m-1)K and increasing mm-suffix ending in a​bab, and let ℓ=b−a−1\ell=b-a-1. Then, letting d=K−md=K-m, we have

|𝒮πm​(j)|=∏i=0j−1(i​d+ℓℓ).|\mathcal{S}_{\pi}^{m}(j)|=\prod_{i=0}^{j-1}\binom{id+\ell}{\ell}.

5.3 Shifted grid posets

There is a standard partial order on the integer lattice ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} where (x,y)(x,y) covers both (x−1,y)(x-1,y) and (x,y−1)(x,y-1) for all xx and yy. Its Hasse diagram can be obtained by rotating this lattice 4545 degrees counterclockwise. We say that the Hasse diagram ℋ\mathcal{H} of a poset 𝒫\mathcal{P} can be embedded in ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} if ℋ\mathcal{H} can be obtained from a connected subset of the Hasse diagram of ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} by adding vertices to some of its edges. An example is given in Figure 5.7.

We now define a particular class of posets that can be embedded in ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} and coincides with a certain class of pattern posets.

Definition 5.29.

Fix m≤K/2m\leq K/2, J≥1J\geq 1 and nonnegative integers h1,…,hm,v1,…,vm−1h_{1},\ldots,h_{m},v_{1},\ldots,v_{m-1}. The shifted grid poset of width JJ with parameters (h1,…,hm:v1,…,vm−1)(h_{1},\ldots,h_{m}:v_{1},\ldots,v_{m-1}) has as Hasse diagram the horizontal lattice segments in the integer lattice ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} from (r,r)(r,r) to (r+J,r)(r+J,r), 1≤r≤m1\leq r\leq m, and the vertical lattice edges between them, directed rightwards and upwards, with hrh_{r} vertices inserted in every horizontal unit edge at height rr, and vrv_{r} vertices in every vertical unit edge from height rr to r+1r+1.

An example of a shifted grid poset and a pattern of the type mentioned in the following theorem is given in Figure 5.7. The corresponding parameters are h1=h2=0,h3=2h_{1}=h_{2}=0,h_{3}=2 and v1=1,v2=0v_{1}=1,v_{2}=0.

Lemma 5.30.

Let π\pi be a KK-pattern, m≤K/2m\leq K/2 and let 𝐝𝐩\mathbf{dp} and 𝐝𝐬\mathbf{ds} be the interiors of the gap vectors of its mm-prefix 𝐩\mathbf{p} and mm-suffix 𝐬\mathbf{s}. The number of simple cycles in 𝒫πm​(2){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(2) equals the number of indices ii such that 𝐝𝐩i\mathbf{dp}_{i} and 𝐝𝐬i\mathbf{ds}_{i} are both positive.

Proof.

A cycle in 𝒫πm​(2){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(2) must have elements from both the first and second lines of its stack, since each line forms a chain in 𝒫πm​(2){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(2). The minimal and maximal elements of such a cycle must belong to both lines, and thus can only be the letters K−m+1,K−m+2,…,KK-m+1,K-m+2,\ldots,K.

By symmetry we may assume that 𝐩\mathbf{p} and 𝐬\mathbf{s} are increasing, so these common letters appear in increasing order on both lines, call them c1<c2<⋯<cmc_{1}<c_{2}<\cdots<c_{m}. Each common letter separates the preceding gaps from the following ones, so a simple cycle cannot extend across an intermediate common letter.

In order for there to be a simple cycle with two of these elements, cic_{i} and ci+1c_{i+1}, as minimum and maximum, there must be, on each of the two lines, a nonempty set of elements strictly between cic_{i} and ci+1c_{i+1}. On the first line, the places of cic_{i} and ci+1c_{i+1} are determined by 𝐬i\mathbf{s}_{i} and 𝐬i+1\mathbf{s}_{i+1}, which must differ by at least 2 in order for there to be some elements strictly between cic_{i} and ci+1c_{i+1} on the first line, which is equivalent to 𝐝𝐬i>0\mathbf{ds}_{i}>0. Conversely, if 𝐝𝐬i=0\mathbf{ds}_{i}=0 then cic_{i} and ci+1c_{i+1} are adjacent on the first line, so there are no letters between them that can form one of the two chains of a cycle in 𝒫πm​(2){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(2).

On the second line, the places of cic_{i} are determined by 𝐩\mathbf{p}, and an analogous argument shows that 𝐝𝐩i\mathbf{dp}_{i} must be positive in order for there to be elements strictly between cic_{i} and ci+1c_{i+1} that contribute to a cycle in 𝒫πm​(2){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(2). ∎

Remark 5.31.

The number of indices ii such that both 𝐝𝐩i\mathbf{dp}_{i} and 𝐝𝐬i\mathbf{ds}_{i} are positive is the first Betti number of the graph of 𝒫πm​(2){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(2) seen as a simplicial complex, that is, equals the rank of its first homology group.

Lemma 5.32.

Let 1<m≤K/21<m\leq K/2. A KK-pattern π\pi whose poset 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) is isomorphic, for every jj, to an mm-level shifted grid poset of width jj with fixed parameters must have 1 in its prefix and KK in its suffix, or vice versa.

Proof.

Note first that a shifted grid poset of width 2 has precisely m−1m-1 simple cycles, the maximum possible for overlap mm, the iith cycle having bottom and top vertices at (i+1,i)(i+1,i) and (i+2,i+1)(i+2,i+1), respectively, for 1≤i<m1\leq i<m. Thus, by Lemma 5.30, the interiors of the gap vectors of both mm-prefix and mm-suffix of π\pi must be positive.

A shifted grid poset has a unique minimal and a unique maximal element, so, by Proposition 5.12, a KK-pattern π\pi with such a poset must have 1 and KK in its mm-prefix or mm-suffix. Suppose 1 and KK both belong to the mm-prefix (the case for the suffix is analogous). Then, by Proposition 5.12, the bottom element of 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j), for any jj, is the first letter of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0} and the top letter is the last letter of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0}. We show that, for any jj, there is a path—a saturated chain—from bottom to top element consisting precisely of the letters of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0}, in that order.

The positivity of the interior of the gap vector of the suffix implies that no two letters shared with 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍1{\mathsf{shift}}_{1} are consecutive in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0}. Thus every consecutive pair in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0} contains a letter occurring on no other line. Such a pair forms a cover relation, since any comparison involving that letter must pass through its predecessor or successor in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0}. Hence 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0} is saturated for every jj.

In a shifted grid poset the length of the shortest path from bottom to top element clearly increases with the number of occurrences jj.

Thus, 1 and KK cannot both belong to the prefix or both to the suffix, so the prefix and suffix must each contain one of 1 and KK. ∎

Theorem 5.33.

Let 1<m≤K/21<m\leq K/2 and let π\pi be a KK-pattern whose mm-prefix 𝐩=p1​p2​…​pm\mathbf{p}=p_{1}p_{2}\ldots p_{m} and mm-suffix 𝐬=s1​s2​…​sm\mathbf{s}=s_{1}s_{2}\ldots s_{m} satisfy

1=p1<s1<p2<s2<⋯<pm<sm=K.1=p_{1}<s_{1}<p_{2}<s_{2}<\cdots<p_{m}<s_{m}=K. (5.4)

Then 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) is a shifted grid poset of width jj with parameters

(h1,h2,…,hm:v1,v2,…,vm−1),(h_{1},h_{2},\ldots,h_{m}:v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{m-1}),

where

hi=si−pi−1​ and ​vi=pi+1−si−1.h_{i}=s_{i}-p_{i}-1\text{ and }v_{i}=p_{i+1}-s_{i}-1. (5.5)

Conversely, given a sequence of shifted grid posets 𝒫j\mathcal{P}_{j} of width jj with the above parameters, let KK be the sum of the hih_{i} and viv_{i} plus 2​m2m, and define 𝐩\mathbf{p} and 𝐬\mathbf{s} recursively by (5.5), starting with p1=1p_{1}=1. Then sm=Ks_{m}=K. Let π=𝐩𝐰𝐬\pi=\mathbf{p}\mathbf{w}\mathbf{s}, where 𝐰\mathbf{w} is any permutation of the letters of [K][K] not in 𝐩\mathbf{p} or 𝐬\mathbf{s}. Then, up to the trivial symmetries in Section 3, π\pi is the only KK-pattern with 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) isomorphic to 𝒫j\mathcal{P}_{j} for every jj.

Proof.

The case j=1j=1 is trivial, so assume j≥2j\geq 2. The first occurrence of π\pi corresponds to a chain in 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) whose order is determined by 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0}. The elements where the chains determined by 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0} and 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍1{\mathsf{shift}}_{1} meet are K−m+1,K−m+2,…,KK-m+1,K-m+2,\ldots,K, as these are precisely the letters shared by 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0} and 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍1{\mathsf{shift}}_{1}.

Because of the interleaving conditions in (5.4) above, the letters 1,2,…,m1,2,\ldots,m and K−m+1,K−m+2,…,KK-m+1,K-m+2,\ldots,K appear in alternating order in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0} (which is the inverse of π\pi):

1≺(K−m+1)≺2≺(K−m+2)≺⋯≺(K−1)≺m≺K,1\prec(K-m+1)\prec 2\prec(K-m+2)\prec\cdots\prec(K-1)\prec m\prec K,

where a≺ba\prec b indicates that aa precedes bb.

Embed the letters 1,2,…,m1,2,\ldots,m and K−m+1,K−m+2,…,KK-m+1,K-m+2,\ldots,K in the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2}-grid so that ii is placed at (i,i)(i,i) and K−m+iK-m+i at (i+1,i)(i+1,i), so that the chain 1,(K−m+1),2,(K−m+2),⋯,(K−1),m,K1,(K-m+1),2,(K-m+2),\cdots,(K-1),m,K forms a zig-zag path starting at (1,1)(1,1) and alternatingly turns up and right after each unit step.

Between the letters ii and K−m+iK-m+i in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0} there may be some letters. The number of such letters is si−pi−1s_{i}-p_{i}-1 and the number of letters between K−m+iK-m+i and i+1i+1 is pi+1−si−1p_{i+1}-s_{i}-1. The set of these letters between ii and K−m+iK-m+i in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0} we place, in the order determined by 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0}, on the horizontal line segment between the places of ii and K−m+iK-m+i in the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2}-lattice, and we likewise place the letters between K−m+iK-m+i and i+1i+1 in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0} on the vertical line segment between K−m+iK-m+i and i+1i+1.

We now construct the analogous zig-zag path in the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2}-grid for the letters in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍1{\mathsf{shift}}_{1}, but starting from (2,1)(2,1). Note that the first letter in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍1{\mathsf{shift}}_{1} is K−m+1K-m+1, which was placed at (2,1)(2,1) when we placed the letters of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0}. Similarly, the letter in place p2p_{2} of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍1{\mathsf{shift}}_{1} is K−m+2K-m+2, which we place at (3,2)(3,2), as we did when placing the letters of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0}, and this holds in general, so the letters in the zig-zag chain for 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍1{\mathsf{shift}}_{1} that coincide with letters in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0} are placed at the same points in ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} as their counterparts in 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0}.

Now, 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍1{\mathsf{shift}}_{1} is order isomorphic to 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0}, and the path in ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} containing the letters of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍1{\mathsf{shift}}_{1} is identical to the path for 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0} shifted one unit to the right. Thus horizontal segments at the same height contain the same number of interior elements, and likewise for vertical segments connecting the same two horizontal rows. Repeating this construction for the remaining lines gives the required shifted grid of width jj.

For the converse it may be helpful to consider the shifted grid poset in Figure 5.7, where (K−m+1,K−m+2,…,K)(K-m+1,K-m+2,\ldots,K), the letters belonging to both 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0} and 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍1{\mathsf{shift}}_{1}, are (7,8,9)(7,8,9).

Summing the defining identities in (5.5) gives that the sum of the hih_{i} and viv_{i} equals sm−2​m,s_{m}-2m, since p1=1p_{1}=1. Thus sm=Ks_{m}=K by the definition of KK.

Let τ\tau be a pattern whose poset 𝒫τn​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\tau}^{n}(j) is isomorphic to 𝒫j\mathcal{P}_{j} for every jj, and let π\pi be the pattern defined in the statement of the theorem. Note that for 𝒫τn​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\tau}^{n}(j) and 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) to have the same number of elements for all jj (indeed for just j=1,2j=1,2), we must have m=nm=n and π\pi and τ\tau must have the same length KK.

Let 𝐩′=p1′​p2′,…​pm′\mathbf{p}^{\prime}=p^{\prime}_{1}p^{\prime}_{2},\ldots p^{\prime}_{m} and 𝐬′=s1′​s2′,…,sm′\mathbf{s}^{\prime}=s^{\prime}_{1}s^{\prime}_{2},\ldots,s^{\prime}_{m} be the mm-prefix and mm-suffix, respectively, of τ\tau, both of which we assume to be increasing, without loss of generality. We will show that 𝐩′=𝐩\mathbf{p}^{\prime}=\mathbf{p} and 𝐬′=𝐬\mathbf{s}^{\prime}=\mathbf{s}, which will complete the proof. We may assume, by Lemma 5.32 and symmetry, that p1′=1p^{\prime}_{1}=1 and sm′=Ks^{\prime}_{m}=K (by definition we also have π=1​…​K\pi=1\ldots K). Let ℋ\mathcal{H} be the embedding of the Hasse diagram of 𝒫τm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\tau}^{m}(j) in ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2}, identical to the embedding of the isomorphic shifted grid poset 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j).

Define the tail of a shifted grid poset to be the chain of elements to the left of the element at (2,1)(2,1) in ℋ\mathcal{H}. (The head is defined analogously, from the top element.) The Hasse diagram ℋ\mathcal{H} of a shifted grid poset 𝒫πm​(2){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(2) consists, apart from tail and head, of m−1m-1 cycles, one for each aa with 1≤a≤m−11\leq a\leq m-1, containing the elements K−m+aK-m+a and K−m+a+1K-m+a+1 together with two disjoint chains between them. This is a consequence of the interiors of the gap vectors of both the mm-prefix and mm-suffix being strictly positive. That positivity of gap vectors is also necessary in order for the Hasse diagram of the poset 𝒫τm​(2){\mathcal{P}}_{\tau}^{m}(2) of any pattern τ\tau to consist of m−1m-1 such cycles, by Lemma 5.30.

Now consider 𝒫τm​(3){\mathcal{P}}_{\tau}^{m}(3). The positivity of the interior of the gap vector of 𝐬′\mathbf{s}^{\prime} implies that each pair of adjacent letters on the first line of the stack for τ\tau contains a letter occurring on no other line. Hence the first line is a saturated chain CC, starting at the bottom element. Only the mm letters CC shares with the second line can have degree greater than two, since every other letter occurs only on the first line. The last letter of CC covers two letters in the topmost cycle of 𝒫τm​(2){\mathcal{P}}_{\tau}^{m}(2). These remain covers when the third line is added, since that line does not contain the last letter. It is covered by just one letter, since the first line ends there and only the second line continues above it.

In 𝒫πm​(3){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(3), a vertex covering two elements and being covered by one vertex lies on the top horizontal row. A saturated chain from the bottom to such a vertex must pass through at least one vertex of degree greater than two on each of the mm rows. Our chain CC can contain at most mm such vertices. Starting from the bottom, it must therefore turn upwards at the first such vertex on each row: continuing to the right would encounter a second one on that row. On the top row it must stop at the first such vertex. Thus the first line follows precisely the leftmost zig-zag in the grid.

The mm letters of 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍0{\mathsf{shift}}_{0} that are shared with 𝗌𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍1{\mathsf{shift}}_{1} consequently occupy the vertices (i+1,i)(i+1,i), for 1≤i≤m1\leq i\leq m. The iith shared letter is in place si′s^{\prime}_{i} on the first line. Its corresponding vertex is in place sis_{i} along the first zig-zag, so si′=sis^{\prime}_{i}=s_{i} for every ii.

Return now to 𝒫πm​(2){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(2) and number the m−1m-1 cycles from bottom to top in each of the two posets. An isomorphism preserves this order, so it matches their iith cycles. Between the iith and (i+1)(i+1)st shared letters, the two sides of the ii-th cycle have si+1′−si′−1s^{\prime}_{i+1}-s^{\prime}_{i}-1 and pi+1′−pi′−1p^{\prime}_{i+1}-p^{\prime}_{i}-1 interior elements, respectively. The corresponding numbers for π\pi are si+1−si−1s_{i+1}-s_{i}-1 and pi+1−pi−1p_{i+1}-p_{i}-1. Since the suffix values already agree, equality of the total numbers of interior elements in the matched cycles gives pi+1′−pi′=pi+1−pip^{\prime}_{i+1}-p^{\prime}_{i}=p_{i+1}-p_{i}. Together with p1′=p1=1p^{\prime}_{1}=p_{1}=1, this gives 𝐩′=𝐩\mathbf{p}^{\prime}=\mathbf{p}, completing the proof. ∎

Remark 5.34.

Although there is (up to trivial symmetries) a unique pattern π\pi for each shifted grid poset with a given set of parameters, there are typically more patterns with the same enumeration because their posets are ’essentially’ isomorphic to the shifted grid poset for π\pi. As an example, the pattern π=1364257\pi=1364257 with overlap 3 has the same enumeration as the pattern 147962358 with overlap 4. The poset 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) for the former is a shifted grid poset and the poset for the latter is obtained from 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) by attaching a chain of length j+1j+1 to the bottom element of 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j), which doesn’t affect the number of linear extensions, because patterns corresponding to shifted grid posets have 1 in prefix and KK in suffix, and their posets therefore have no branches, by Porism 5.17, so the elements of this attached chain are comparable to all the elements of the poset and must therefore be a prefix of any linear extension.

There is an example of a shifted grid poset, for the pattern 513624 with overlap 3 in [5, Fig. 1]. This pattern is equivalent (by sorting prefix and suffix) to 135246, and the poset has all parameters 0.

Corollary 5.35.

Let (h1,h2,…,hm:v1,v2,…,vm−1)(h_{1},h_{2},\ldots,h_{m}:v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{m-1}) be the parameters of a shifted grid poset whose corresponding pattern π\pi has length KK. Then, setting vm=0v_{m}=0, we have

∑i=1m(hi+vi)=K−2​m.\sum_{i=1}^{m}(h_{i}+v_{i})=K-2m. (5.6)
Proof.

Summing the identities in (5.5), and using p1=1p_{1}=1, sm=Ks_{m}=K and vm=0v_{m}=0, gives

∑i=1m(hi+vi)=sm−p1−(2​m−1)=K−2​m.∎\sum_{i=1}^{m}(h_{i}+v_{i})=s_{m}-p_{1}-(2m-1)=K-2m.\qed

We single out a specific subclass of shifted grid posets, given by two levels—henceforth termed the shifted two-level posets and therefore parametrized by a triple (h,v,h′)=(h1,v1,h2)(h,v,h^{\prime})=(h_{1},v_{1},h_{2}) of non-negative integers. These posets are straightforward to characterize, as follows.

Corollary 5.36.

Fix h1,v1,h2≥0h_{1},v_{1},h_{2}\geq 0 and let π\pi be a KK-pattern whose 2-packing poset for every j≥1j\geq 1 is isomorphic to the two-level shifted grid poset of width jj with parameters (h1,h2:v1)(h_{1},h_{2}:v_{1}). Then, up to trivial symmetries, π1=1\pi_{1}=1, π2=h1+v1+3\pi_{2}=h_{1}+v_{1}+3, πK−1=h1+2\pi_{K-1}=h_{1}+2, and πK=K\pi_{K}=K.

Proof.

By Theorem 5.33, up to trivial symmetries, a pattern of this kind must have π1=1\pi_{1}=1 and πK=K\pi_{K}=K. Thus we have

h1=πK−1−2,v1=π2−πK−1−1.h_{1}=\pi_{K-1}-2,\qquad v_{1}=\pi_{2}-\pi_{K-1}-1.

Therefore πK−1=h1+2\pi_{K-1}=h_{1}+2 and π2=h1+v1+3\pi_{2}=h_{1}+v_{1}+3. ∎

A special case of the patterns in Corollary 5.36, when K≥5K\geq 5, are those with prefix 1313 and suffix 2​K2K, for which h=v=0,h′=K−4h=v=0,h^{\prime}=K-4. The following proposition is essentially derived via generating functions in [8, Theorem 4.2], except that there the interfix is taken to be increasing and the pattern has (K+1)​(K+2)​…​(2​K−5)(K+1)(K+2)\ldots(2K-5) appended to it, and the overlap is K−3K-3. The posets in question differ only in that the one for the longer pattern has K−5K-5 more elements in its head, and thus they trivially have the same enumeration of linear extensions.

Proposition 5.37.

The number of permutations that 22-pack jj occurrences of the KK-pattern with prefix 1313 and suffix 2​K2K, where K≥4K\geq 4, is the generalized Catalan number 1(K−3)​j+1​((K−2)​jj)\frac{1}{(K-3)j+1}\binom{(K-2)j}{j}.

When K=4K=4 the pattern is 1324, whose poset is the smallest nontrivial shifted grid poset, and whose enumeration is the Catalan number CjC_{j}. That result was obtained already by Liese and Remmel in [13]; see also [8, Section 4.1]. Interestingly, the case K=4K=4 of Proposition 5.37, with overlap 2, has the same enumeration as the pattern π(a)=1​(a+1)​2​(a+2)​…​a​(2​a)\pi^{(a)}=1(a+1)2(a+2)\ldots a(2a) for any a≥2a\geq 2, with overlap K−2K-2, where K=2​aK=2a. That is straightforward to prove, because the poset for π(a)\pi^{(a)} is obtained from that for 1324 by adding a−2a-2 elements to the tail and to the head of the poset for 1324.

In our forthcoming paper [2] we give an explicit formula for the general case of two-level grid posets.

6 Pattern cover with varying overlap size

So far, the special cases considered involve pattern packing with a fixed overlap mm. For some classes of patterns, we observe a further decoupling that allows us to more directly ‘upgrade’ the results obtained for regular overlaps to arbitrary ones. In particular, let π\pi be a KK-pattern with auto-correlation at least 2. Tracking only the occurrences of π\pi arising from overlaps of sizes 11 and 22, we can express the vector of successive overlaps in terms of runs of 1s and 2s as

1¯r1,2¯q1,…,1¯ra,2¯qa\underline{1}_{r_{1}},\underline{2}_{q_{1}},\ldots,\underline{1}_{r_{a}},\underline{2}_{q_{a}}

where a≥1a\geq 1, r1,qa≥0r_{1},q_{a}\geq 0, and qi,ri+1≥1q_{i},r_{i+1}\geq 1 for 1≤i<a1\leq i<a and x¯n\underline{x}_{n} is the word x,…,xx,\ldots,x of length nn (or the empty word when n=0n=0).

Proposition 6.1.

Let π\pi be a KK-pattern of the form 1​σ​K1\sigma K with K≥3K\geq 3. Let 1¯r1,2¯q1,…,1¯ra,2¯qa\underline{1}_{r_{1}},\underline{2}_{q_{1}},\ldots,\underline{1}_{r_{a}},\underline{2}_{q_{a}} specify all successive prescribed overlaps, disregarding potential additional occurrences. Then the number of such permutations is given by the product

Nq1⋅Nq2⋅⋯⋅Nqa,N_{q_{1}}\cdot N_{q_{2}}\cdot\cdots\cdot N_{q_{a}},

where Nq=|𝒮π2​(q+1)|N_{q}=|\mathcal{S}_{\pi}^{2}(q+1)| for any q≥0q\geq 0.

Proof.

Given a permutation σ\sigma of this form we claim that the letter ℓ\ell of the leftmost overlap of size 1 in σ\sigma is greater than all letters preceding ℓ\ell. Now, ℓ\ell is clearly greater than all the letters in the occurrence of π\pi of which ℓ\ell is the last letter. Therefore, if this occurrence overlaps in two letters with a preceding occurrence, ℓ\ell is larger than both letters in that overlap. In particular, it is larger than the last letter of that overlap, which in turn is greater than all other letters in that preceding occurrence. An inductive argument now shows that ℓ\ell must be greater than all the letters preceding it in σ\sigma. An analogous argument shows that ℓ\ell is smaller than all letters following it in σ\sigma.

This determines which subset of letters of σ\sigma belongs to each of the segments between successive 1-overlaps in σ\sigma. A segment between two successive 1-overlaps is thus a permutation covered by π\pi with overlaps 2, whose number is NiN_{i} where ii is the number of 2-overlaps in that segment. Since the ordering of letters in such a segment is independent of the ordering in any other such the proof follows. ∎

Therefore, for π=1324\pi=1324, for example, which can have overlaps of sizes 1 and 2 only, we obtain the full analogue of the enumeration by descent set where we count permutations with occurrences of π\pi in arbitrary prescribed positions, using Proposition 5.37:

Corollary 6.2.

The number of permutations σ\sigma with occurrences of the consecutive pattern 1324 prescribed by the overlaps 1¯r1,2¯q1,…,1¯ra,2¯qa\underline{1}_{r_{1}},\underline{2}_{q_{1}},\ldots,\underline{1}_{r_{a}},\underline{2}_{q_{a}} is

Cq1+1⋅Cq2+1⋅⋯⋅Cqa+1.C_{q_{1}+1}\cdot C_{q_{2}+1}\cdot\cdots\cdot C_{q_{a}+1}.

For non-overlapping occurrences, the picture is even simpler; see Remark 4.8.

7 Open problems, questions and remarks

1.  Lemma 5.10 and Theorems 5.11, 5.16 and 5.18 provide restrictions that apply to all pattern posets. Is it possible to give a complete characterization?

2.  For which pattern-overlap combinations can we generalize Proposition 6.1 about varying overlaps?

3.  Obviously we can, in a trivial sense, compute the enumeration for a pattern from its gap vectors, since they determine prefix and suffix (see the paragraph preceding Theorem 5.23). For the patterns in Proposition 5.25 the product formula is easily computed directly from the gap vectors and the same is true of the patterns in Proposition 5.28. Are there other classes of patterns whose enumeration can be derived in reasonably simple ways from their gap vectors?

4.  We have the following conjecture on the maximum number of permutations (m,j)(m,j)-packing a KK-pattern as a function of (K,m,j)(K,m,j):

Conjecture 7.1.

For overlap m≤K/2m\leq K/2, the maximum is obtained when prefix and suffix are interleaved and minimal, that is, for patterns with prefix 135​…​(2​m−1)135\ldots(2m-1) and suffix 246​…​(2​m)246\ldots(2m).

It is straightforward to show that for jj occurrences a poset of this kind is obtained from the shifted grid poset for jj occurrences of the pattern 13​…​(2​m−1)​24​…​(2​m)13\ldots(2m-1)24\ldots(2m) by adding branches of length K−2​mK-2m going up from the maximum element of each occurrence.

For overlap m=1m=1, the conjectured maximizing pattern has prefix 1 and suffix 2, which, incidentally, was shown in [7] to be the asymptotically most avoided consecutive pattern among those whose occurrences can overlap in at most one place.

For m>K/2m>K/2, the maximizing posets seem to have a structure quite similar to the grid structure of shifted grid posets, and in some cases they are isomorphic to shifted grid posets apart from having longer head/tail.

5.  A separator is an element zz comparable to every element of the poset and whose removal splits the poset into two nonempty subposets, neither of which is a chain. The number of linear extensions of such a poset is the product of the numbers for each subposet. Can we characterize patterns whose posets 𝒫πm​(j){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}^{m}(j) have a separator for j>mj>m? It seems that there is always a separator (namely KK) for overlap 2 if the 2-prefix is 1​a1a and the 2-suffix is b​cbc, where 2<a<b<c−1<K−22<a<b<c-1<K-2. For 135268479135268479 with overlap 33 and j=4j=4 there are three separators; for 479258136479258136 with overlap 66 and j=7j=7 there are five.

6.  The Wilf class in Proposition 5.25, with enumeration (2j−1)!2(2j-1)!_{2}: 1,3,15,105,…1,3,15,105,\ldots seems to contain, for any given overlap m>2m>2, a pattern of any length K>2​mK>2m. Can we find a uniformly described set of representatives, one for each length?

Similar statements seem to apply to other sequences of shifted factorials of the form (dj−c)!d(dj-c)!_{d} and in fact many other sequences. The same can be said of the class whose enumeration is the Catalan numbers. Here is a handful of pattern-overlap combinations in that class, whose posets only differ by the lengths of their heads and tails:

1324-2
14253-3
136245-3
142536-4
1376245-3
369247815-5
162738495-7

What kind of operations on patterns might explain this?

7.  Our computations for KK up to 12 suggest22 2 These results are from running programs to compute the numbers of permutations covered by each pattern for each possible overlap between 1 and K−2K-2, and up to at least 77 occurrences. In these data, any two pattern-overlap combinations whose enumerations differ for seven occurrences differ already for five occurrences. Overlap K−1K-1 is ignored, since that implies that a KK-pattern π\pi is increasing or decreasing, with exactly one permutation of each length n≥Kn\geq K covered by π\pi. We have not tried to verify rigorously that our programming is correct, but comparisons with other methods of computing this have yielded no discrepancies. that there are 31,111 combinations of KK-patterns and overlaps that are inequivalent modulo the symmetries in Section 3, and 10,787 distinct initial enumerating sequences for these. Of these combinations, 2,684 have the trivial sequence 1,1,1,…1,1,1,\ldots because the poset in question is a chain. Of the remaining ones 452 have initial terms matching (2n)n≥0(2^{n})_{n\geq 0}, 385 matching (3n)n≥0(3^{n})_{n\geq 0}, 374 matching the Catalan numbers and 331 matching the sequence (3​nn)/(2​n+1)\binom{3n}{n}/(2n+1) for n≥0n\geq 0. Other sequences appear for fewer than 300 pattern-overlap combinations each, and there are over 1,000 such combinations that have a unique enumeration.

Here n=j−1n=j-1 for the power sequences, and n=jn=j for the Catalan and Fuss–Catalan sequences. Agreement of finitely many terms of course does not establish Wilf equivalence, but it seems unlikely that any sequences in these data that agree up to seven occurrences will split later.

Although we have not analyzed this exhaustively, it seems that for most of these apparent Wilf classes (sets of pattern-overlap combinations with the same enumeration) the posets in question are isomorphic, apart from the number and placement of elements that belong to head or tail, or else cover and are covered by a single element, and are comparable to all elements of the poset. Such elements don’t affect the number of linear extensions. One exception to this is the triple of patterns 125634 and 163425 with overlap 2 and 167359248 with overlap 3 (see Figure 5.6), and it would be interesting to find further such nontrivial Wilf classes.

8.  As mentioned in the footnote to item 7, if two pattern-overlap combinations have different enumeration for 1-7 occurrences, for patterns of length up to 12, then they have different enumeration already for five occurrences. Is it possible that 5 is a cutoff for any pair of patterns, of arbitrary lengths, or that there is at least a small such bound that depends only on pattern length?

9.  The Wilf class with enumeration sequence 2j−12^{j-1} contains, among an apparent infinity of pattern-overlap combinations, 132546-2, 1324657-2 and 123584679-4. All can be explained by straightforward arguments showing that on each pair of successive lines of the stack there is a pair of elements that are incomparable to each other, but otherwise all elements are comparable. All pattern posets we have seen with this enumeration consist of cycles where two such incomparable elements are the only deviation from the poset being a chain. Similar posets seem to exist for the sequence knk^{n} for any positive kk, and for an infinite collection of pattern-overlap combinations in each case.

It seems plausible that understanding some of these Wilf equivalences will lead to greater understanding than just for each class. For anybody interested in exploring these and other Wilf equivalences we are happy to share both our data and the python code we have used to compute the enumeration.

10.  In our enumeration data mentioned in item 7 above, just over a third of the sequences have a product formula. Many of these formulas have factors that are single binomial coefficients, such as in Propositions 5.25 and 5.28. This is not true in general. The enumeration for 135289467 with overlap 3, for example, has a product formula according to our data, but the successive factors are not single binomial coefficients. However, the factors are polynomial starting from j=3j=3, namely 121​(j−30)+168​(j−31)+72​(j−32)121\binom{j-3}{0}+168\binom{j-3}{1}+72\binom{j-3}{2}, in the binomial basis. All the product formulas in our data have such polynomial factors.

11.  A curiosity in the enumeration for 14325 with overlap 2 is that all the numbers are congruent to 6 mod 10, except when j=2k−1j=2^{k}-1, those are congruent to 1. This holds at least up to 23 occurrences and we see no obvious reason for that looking at the prime factorizations:
